# Overview

In Exercises 4 and 5, one variable, GDP per capita, was used to test whether counties with similar
values are neighbours. This exercise uses six variables on information and communication technology
(ICT), five of them in the clustering, for a different question: can the 55 townships of Shan State,
Myanmar, be grouped into a small number of regions, each made of townships with similar access to
ICT, and each a single connected piece of territory?

Such a grouping is called regionalisation or geographic segmentation. On slide 3, regions are
defined as internally homogeneous and contiguous, which combines two requirements:

- from cluster analysis, that the townships in a region are similar on the variables;
- from spatial analysis, that a region is one connected piece, so that it can be mapped and managed
  as one area.

**Part 1** is a reproduction of r4gdsa chapter 12: the data, exploratory analysis, conventional
hierarchical clustering, the SKATER and ClustGeo methods of spatially constrained clustering, and
the profiles of the clusters. **Part 2** is a review of the chapter's method, with the methods on
the Lesson 6 slides that the chapter does not cover: REDCAP, the automatic zoning procedure (AZP)
and max-p. Spatially constrained hierarchical clustering (SCHC) is included as well. It is not on
the slides, and it is provided by the `rgeoda` package used for the other three.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}

## Sources

The hands-on exercise is one chapter, assigned for Lesson 6:

- [Chapter 12: Geographical Segmentation with Spatially Constrained Clustering
  Techniques](https://r4gdsa.netlify.app/chap12.html)

The Lesson 6 outline sets two papers as self-reading.

| Reading | What it contributes | Used in |
|--------|--------------|----|
| **Assunção et al. (2006)**, "Efficient Regionalization Techniques for Socio-Economic Geographical Units Using Minimum Spanning Trees" | SKATER: the minimum spanning tree and the conditions for its uniqueness, the pruning of the tree into regions, attributes measured "in standard deviation units", a one-district region in the unrestricted São Paulo result and the minimum-population restriction that removes it, a comparison with AZP, the sum of squared deviations within regions as the quality of a partition, and the debate on combining homogeneity with compactness | Part 2, 3.2, 4.2, 4.5, 4.6, 4.7 |
| **Chavent et al. (2018)**, "ClustGeo: an R package for hierarchical clustering with spatial constraints" | The Ward-like criterion on two dissimilarity matrices, the choice of α, the equivalence of `hclustgeo()` with `hclust(method = "ward.D")` on the transformed matrix, the two kinds of geographic matrix D1, and the proportion of explained pseudo-inertia | Part 2, 3.3, 4.3, 4.6 |

The outline also lists five references. All five are used on this page:

| Reference | What it contributes | Used in |
|--------|--------------|----|
| **Rovan and Sambt (2003)**, "Socio-economic Differences Among Slovenian Municipalities: A Cluster Analysis Approach" | All variables standardised, with the remark that the method makes no distributional assumptions; the number of clusters read from jumps in the Ward merge heights; clusters named from their mean profiles | 4.2, 4.4, 4.8 |
| **Demeter and Brătucu (2013)**, "Statistical Analysis of the EU Countries from a Touristic Point of View" | Cluster membership read at two, three and four clusters from one tree, showing how the hierarchy nests | 4.4 |
| **Brown and Watson (2012)**, "What can a comprehensive plan really tell us about a region?" | The rule of thumb k = √(n/2); cluster means expressed as a percentage of the overall mean; clusters described by variables that were not used to form them | 4.4, 4.8 |
| **Jaya et al. (2019)**, "Clustering with spatial constraints: The case of diarrhea in Bandung city, Indonesia" | ClustGeo with a distance-based and a contiguity-based D1 on the same data, and the argument that the choice of D1 should follow how the phenomenon spreads | 4.6 |
| **de Souza and Taconeli (2022)**, "Spatial and non-spatial clustering algorithms in the analysis of Brazilian educational data" | A Moran's I test on each variable before clustering; one k for every method; ClustGeo with both kinds of D1 and SKATER compared on the same data; clusters cross-tabulated against official regions and compared by F tests; min-max scaling; the NbClust majority vote for the number of clusters | 4.1, 4.2, 4.4, 4.6, 4.8 |

The outline's "All About R" section has links to four web pages, and three of them are used on this
page. The UC Business Analytics tutorial on hierarchical cluster analysis is the source of chapter
sections 12.7.8 to 12.7.10, and is used in sections 3.1.8, 4.2, 4.3 and 4.4. The `spdep` reference
for `skater()` documents the population criterion used in section 4.5, and the ClustGeo introduction
page documents the two kinds of D1 used in section 4.6.

The Lesson 6 slide deck, dated 18 September 2026, lists five methods. The chapter covers two of
them, SKATER and ClustGeo. REDCAP (slides 9 to 12), AZP and max-p (slide 2) are covered in section
4.7.

## Differences from the chapter

| | The chapter | This page | Why | Where |
|-------|---------|----------|--------------------|----|
| **Scale of the clustering variables** | computes min-max and z-score versions in 12.7.3 and 12.7.4, then clusters on the raw rates | Part 1 follows the chapter; Part 2 repeats the analysis on z-scores | On the raw rates, mobile phone and TV account for 81% of the squared distance between townships and computer for 0.6%. Standardising changes the six clusters substantially (adjusted Rand index 0.32) | 4.2 |
| **Ward's method** | picks Ward from `agnes()`, then runs `hclust(method = "ward.D")` | `ward.D2`, which is the method `agnes()` scored and the one `hclustgeo()` runs | `agnes(method = "ward")` and `hclust(method = "ward.D2")` build identical trees. `ward.D` applied to unsquared distances is a different algorithm, and it changes the cluster sizes | 4.3 |
| **Spatial pattern of each variable** | not tested | Moran's I for each of the six rates, as de Souza and Taconeli (2022) do before clustering | Only radio and land line are significantly autocorrelated. TV and mobile phone, which have the most weight in the raw distances, show no significant spatial pattern | 4.1 |
| **Number of clusters** | k = 1 has the largest gap statistic, and 6 is taken as having "the largest gap statistic" after it | 6 kept, with the evidence from five criteria listed | k = 1 has the largest gap. NbClust's majority vote is 2. Ward's merge heights, read as Rovan and Sambt (2003) read them, jump at 2, 4 and 6 | 4.4 |
| **SKATER singletons** | six regions, two of them single townships, not discussed | the singletons identified, and a minimum number of households per region applied, as in Assunção et al. (2006) | Three of six SKATER regions on the standardised variables are single townships: Muse, Tachileik and Taunggyi | 4.5 |
| **Geographic matrix D1 for ClustGeo** | `st_distance()` between polygons | centroid distances and the neighbourhood matrix of Chavent et al. (2018) compared | The distance between two polygons that share a boundary is zero. All 132 neighbouring pairs, and only those pairs, have D1 = 0, so D1 gives every neighbour the same value, zero, whatever the distance between their centres | 4.6 |
| **Contiguity of the result** | reported from the map | counted | ClustGeo applies a soft constraint. The chapter's α = 0.2 solution has six clusters in 18 separate pieces | 4.6, 4.8 |
| **REDCAP, SCHC, AZP, max-p** | not covered | computed with `rgeoda` and compared | Slides 2 and 10 to 12 list REDCAP, AZP and max-p; SCHC is added from `rgeoda` | 4.7 |
| **Minimum spanning tree** | `mstree()` without a seed | `set.seed()` before `mstree()` | `mstree()` starts from a random node. The tree is the same, but the printed order of its edges and the numbering of the SKATER groups change from run to run | 3.2.3 |
| **Colours for six groups** | `rect.hclust(border = 2:5)` and `groups.colors` with five colours | six colours | With fewer colours than groups, the colours are reused and two groups look like one | 3.1.10, 3.2.4 |
| **Cluster profiles** | the chapter profiles the non-spatial ClustGeo clusters (12.10) | the profiles are drawn for the spatially constrained clusters as well | The purpose of the chapter is the regions, and the non-spatial clusters are fragmented | 3.4, 4.8 |

# Getting started

## Packages

`rgeoda` provides the four methods in section 4.7, and `mclust` provides the adjusted Rand index
used in Part 2 to compare two sets of clusters.

```{r}
pacman::p_load(spdep, tmap, sf, ClustGeo, rgeoda,
               ggpubr, cluster, factoextra, NbClust,
               heatmaply, corrplot, psych, GGally, mclust,
               knitr, tidyverse)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
The block uses one function:

```r
pacman::p_load(...)                                       # pacman
```

- `p_load()` installs any package that is missing and then attaches all of them, so one call
  replaces a series of `install.packages()` and `library()` calls.

Two of the packages define a function with the same name. `spdep` and `rgeoda` both have a
`skater()`, and whichever package is attached later hides the other. This page therefore always
writes `spdep::skater()` or `rgeoda::skater()` in full.

| Package | Used for |
|-------|-------------|
| `sf`, `spdep` | reading the boundaries, the neighbour list, the minimum spanning tree and SKATER |
| `tidyverse` | reading and reshaping the table, and `ggplot2` charts |
| `tmap` | choropleth maps |
| `corrplot`, `psych`, `ggpubr`, `GGally` | correlation plot, descriptive statistics, arranged charts, parallel coordinates |
| `cluster`, `factoextra`, `NbClust` | agglomerative coefficient, gap statistic, cluster-number indices |
| `heatmaply` | min-max standardisation and the cluster heatmap |
| `ClustGeo` | Ward-like clustering with a geographic constraint |
| `rgeoda` | REDCAP, SCHC, AZP and max-p (Part 2) |
| `mclust`, `knitr` | adjusted Rand index; tables (Part 2) |
:::

## The data

Both files come from the Myanmar Information Management Unit (MIMU), according to section 12.3, and
are distributed with the exercise on eLearn.

| Layer | Format | Features | Native CRS | Contents |
|----|---|---|----|------|
| `myanmar_township_boundaries` | ESRI shapefile | 330 polygons | WGS 84, EPSG:4326 | Township boundaries of Myanmar |
| `Shan-ICT` | CSV | 55 rows, 11 fields | not spatial | Households owning each ICT item, 2014 Population and Housing Census |

### Township boundaries

```{r}
#| results: hide
shan_sf <- st_read(dsn = "data/geospatial",
                   layer = "myanmar_township_boundaries") |>
  filter(ST %in% c("Shan (East)", "Shan (North)", "Shan (South)")) |>
  select(c(2:7))
```

```{r}
shan_sf
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
The block uses three functions:

```r
st_read(dsn, layer)                                       # sf
filter(.data, ...)                                        # dplyr
select(.data, ...)                                        # dplyr
```

- `st_read()` reads the shapefile into an sf data frame with one row per township. `dsn` is the
  folder and `layer` the file name without its extension. It prints a summary that begins with the
  full path of the data folder on the computer that renders the page, and the chunk option
  `results: hide` keeps that summary off the page.
- `filter()` keeps the rows for which a condition is true. The condition here is
  `ST %in% c("Shan (East)", "Shan (North)", "Shan (South)")`, dissected below.
- `select(c(2:7))` keeps columns 2 to 7 by position, also dissected below.

**What `ST`, `DT` and `TS` are**

Myanmar is divided into states and regions, each state or region into districts, and each district
into townships. The file has one row per township, 330 rows, and three of its columns record the
state, the district and the township name of each row:

<div style="border: 2px solid #6c757d; border-radius: 6px; padding: 0.6em 0.8em; max-width: 30em; margin: 1em auto;">
<b><code>ST</code></b>: state or region, for example <code>Shan (North)</code>
<div style="border: 2px solid #6c757d; border-radius: 6px; padding: 0.6em 0.8em; margin-top: 0.5em;">
<b><code>DT</code></b>: district within the state, for example <code>Mongmit</code>
<div style="border: 2px solid #6c757d; border-radius: 6px; padding: 0.6em 0.8em; margin-top: 0.5em; background: #f8f9fa;">
<b><code>TS</code></b>: township within the district, for example <code>Mongmit</code>. One township is one row of the file.
</div></div></div>

A district and a township can share a name, as Mongmit does. The file also splits Shan State into
three parts, `Shan (North)`, `Shan (South)` and `Shan (East)`, and records each part in `ST` as if
it were a separate state. That is why the filter has to name all three.

**The `filter()` line, step by step**

The filter is applied below to three of the 330 rows.

<table class="table table-sm" style="width: auto; margin: 0 auto;">
<tr><th style="background: rgba(13, 110, 253, 0.18);"><code>ST</code></th><th><code>DT</code></th><th><code>TS</code></th></tr>
<tr><td style="background: rgba(255, 193, 7, 0.45);">Shan (North)</td><td>Mongmit</td><td>Mongmit</td></tr>

<pre style="width: auto; margin: 0 auto; padding: 0.6em;"><code>filter(<span style="border-bottom: 2px solid #0d6efd;">ST %in% c(&quot;Shan (East)&quot;, <span style="background: rgba(255, 193, 7, 0.45);">&quot;Shan (North)&quot;</span>, <span style="background: rgba(255, 193, 7, 0.45);">&quot;Shan (South)&quot;</span>)</span>)</code></pre>

<tr style="background: rgba(25, 135, 84, 0.15);"><td>Shan (South)</td><td>Taunggyi</td><td>Pindaya</td><td>kept</td></tr>

Applied to all 330 rows, the same steps keep the 55 townships of Shan State.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| results: hide
mmr_all <- st_read(dsn = "data/geospatial", layer = "myanmar_township_boundaries")
mmr_names <- names(mmr_all)
shan_parts <- c("Shan (East)", "Shan (North)", "Shan (South)")
```

The map shows the three parts among the 18 values of `ST`:

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 4.6
mmr_all <- mmr_all |> mutate(part = if_else(ST %in% shan_parts, ST, "other states"))
part_cols <- c(`Shan (East)` = "#1b9e77", `Shan (North)` = "#d95f02", `Shan (South)` = "#7570b3",
               `other states` = "grey85")
map_parts <- ggplot(mmr_all) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = part), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.05) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = part_cols, breaks = names(part_cols)) +
  labs(fill = "value of ST") + theme_void()
bar_parts <- mmr_all |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  count(ST, part) |>
  ggplot(aes(n, reorder(ST, n), fill = part)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = part_cols, guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "townships", y = NULL)
patchwork::wrap_plots(map_parts, bar_parts, widths = c(1.1, 1))
```

The same condition can be written without `%in%`, as one comparison per name joined by `|`, which
means "or":

```r
filter(ST == "Shan (East)" | ST == "Shan (North)" | ST == "Shan (South)")
```

`%in%` compares whole values, so each name must match exactly, including the space and the brackets.
`ST %in% "Shan"` matches `r sum(mmr_all$ST %in% "Shan")` townships, because no value of `ST` is the
word "Shan" on its own.

**The `select()` line**

`select(c(2:7))` keeps columns by their position in the file, so the position of each column has to
be known first. RStudio's data viewer numbers the rows but not the columns, so the positions are
easiest to read in the Console.

`names()` prints the column names in order. The number in square brackets at the start of each
printed line is the position of the first name on that line:

```r
st_read(dsn = "data/geospatial", layer = "myanmar_township_boundaries") |> names()
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
mmr_names
```

`ST` is the second name on the line that starts at `[1]`, so it is column 2. `TS_PCODE` is the
second name on the line that starts at `[6]`, so it is column 7.

For a file with many columns, putting the names into a data frame prints one name per line, with its
position as the row number:

```r
col_names <- st_read(dsn = "data/geospatial", layer = "myanmar_township_boundaries") |> names()
data.frame(names = col_names)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
data.frame(names = mmr_names)
```

The file has 15 columns, and positions 2 to 7 are the shaded ones:

```{r}
#| echo: false
cols <- mmr_names[1:15]
kept <- seq_along(cols) %in% 2:7
cells <- ifelse(kept, sprintf('<td style="background: rgba(255, 193, 7, 0.30)">%s</td>', cols),
                sprintf("<td>%s</td>", cols))
nums <- ifelse(kept, sprintf('<th style="background: rgba(255, 193, 7, 0.30)">%d</th>', seq_along(cols)),
               sprintf("<th>%d</th>", seq_along(cols)))
htmltools::HTML(paste0('<table class="table table-sm" style="font-size: 0.8em;"><tr>',
                       paste(nums, collapse = ""), "</tr><tr>", paste(cells, collapse = ""),
                       "</tr></table>"))
```

The six kept columns are the state (`ST`), district (`DT`) and township (`TS`) names, each with its
code (`_PCODE`). Column 15, `geometry`, is not listed but is kept, because `select()` on an sf
object always keeps the geometry.

The same six columns can be selected by name, which does not depend on the column order and names
the kept columns in the code:

```r
select(ST, ST_PCODE, DT, DT_PCODE, TS, TS_PCODE)
```
:::

The layer is left in longitude and latitude, as in the chapter. Contiguity is defined by shared
boundaries and does not depend on the projection.

### ICT indicators

```{r}
ict <- read_csv("data/aspatial/Shan-ICT.csv")
summary(ict)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
The block uses two functions:

```r
read_csv(file)                                            # readr
summary(object)                                           # base R
```

- `read_csv()` reads the CSV into a tibble, a kind of data frame, and guesses the type of each
  column from its values. It reports those guesses in a message, which the page setting
  `message: false` keeps off the page.
- `summary()` prints the minimum, quartiles, mean and maximum of each numeric column.
:::

::: callout-note
## What the ICT table contains

ICT stands for information and communication technology: the devices and services a household uses
to receive information and to communicate. The chapter also calls the variables "InfoComm", a
shorter name for the same thing.

The table is an extract of the 2014 Myanmar Population and Housing Census for the 55 townships of
Shan State. Each row is one township, and the eleven columns are in three groups. Three rows of the
file:

<table class="table table-sm" style="font-size: 0.85em;">
<tr>
<th colspan="4" style="background: rgba(13, 110, 253, 0.15); text-align: center;">Which township</th>
<th style="background: rgba(108, 117, 125, 0.18); text-align: center;">How many households</th>
<th colspan="6" style="background: rgba(25, 135, 84, 0.15); text-align: center;">How many of those households own each item</th>
</tr>
<tr>
<th>District Pcode</th><th>District Name</th><th>Township Pcode</th><th>Township Name</th>
<th>Total households</th>
<th>Radio</th><th>Television</th><th>Land line phone</th><th>Mobile phone</th><th>Computer</th><th>Internet at home</th>
</tr>
<tr><td>MMR014D001</td><td>Taunggyi</td><td>MMR014001</td><td>Taunggyi</td><td>82,604</td><td>30,176</td><td>62,388</td><td>6,736</td><td>48,461</td><td>6,705</td><td>9,746</td></tr>
<tr><td>MMR014D001</td><td>Taunggyi</td><td>MMR014002</td><td>Nyaungshwe</td><td>42,634</td><td>13,801</td><td>23,640</td><td>810</td><td>14,973</td><td>669</td><td>1,604</td></tr>
<tr><td>MMR015D007</td><td>Matman</td><td>MMR015024</td><td>Matman</td><td>3,318</td><td>810</td><td>728</td><td>28</td><td>150</td><td>20</td><td>15</td></tr>
</table>

The first row reads: Taunggyi township, in Taunggyi district, has 82,604 households, and 30,176 of
them own a radio, 62,388 a television, and so on across the six items. Matman, the smallest
township, has 3,318 households.

The `Township Pcode` column holds the same codes as `TS_PCODE` in the boundary file, and section 2.4
joins the two tables on it. Section 2.3 turns the six counts into rates, because a count of radios
in Taunggyi and one in Matman are counts out of very different numbers of households.
:::

## Penetration rates

A township with more households has more households with a radio, whatever the level of access. In
section 12.4.3, each count is divided by the number of households and multiplied by 1,000, which
gives the number of households per thousand that own the item.

```{r}
ict_derived <- ict |>
  mutate(RADIO_PR = Radio / `Total households` * 1000,
         TV_PR = Television / `Total households` * 1000,
         LLPHONE_PR = `Land line phone` / `Total households` * 1000,
         MPHONE_PR = `Mobile phone` / `Total households` * 1000,
         COMPUTER_PR = Computer / `Total households` * 1000,
         INTERNET_PR = `Internet at home` / `Total households` * 1000) |>
  rename(DT_PCODE = `District Pcode`, DT = `District Name`,
         TS_PCODE = `Township Pcode`, TS = `Township Name`,
         TT_HOUSEHOLDS = `Total households`,
         RADIO = Radio, TV = Television,
         LLPHONE = `Land line phone`, MPHONE = `Mobile phone`,
         COMPUTER = Computer, INTERNET = `Internet at home`)

summary(ict_derived[, 12:17])
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
The block uses two functions:

```r
mutate(.data, ...)                                        # dplyr
rename(.data, new_name = old_name, ...)                   # dplyr
```

- `mutate()` adds new columns computed from existing ones. The chapter writes a separate `mutate()`
  call for each of the six rates. A single `mutate()` call with six arguments gives the same result.
- A column name that contains a space has to be written between backticks, as in ``
  `Total households` ``. That is the reason for the `rename()` that follows.
- `rename()` gives the columns short names without spaces, written `new = old`.
- `ict_derived[, 12:17]` uses R's square brackets, which pick part of a table in the form
  `table[rows, columns]`. Nothing before the comma means every row, and `12:17` after the comma
  means columns 12 to 17. `mutate()` adds the six rates after the eleven original columns, so they
  are columns 12 to 17:

```{r}
#| echo: false
cols17 <- names(ict_derived)
kept17 <- seq_along(cols17) %in% 12:17
cells17 <- ifelse(kept17, sprintf('<td style="background: rgba(255, 193, 7, 0.30)">%s</td>', cols17),
                  sprintf("<td>%s</td>", cols17))
nums17 <- ifelse(kept17, sprintf('<th style="background: rgba(255, 193, 7, 0.30)">%d</th>', seq_along(cols17)),
                 sprintf("<th>%d</th>", seq_along(cols17)))
htmltools::HTML(paste0('<div style="overflow-x: auto;"><table class="table table-sm" style="font-size: 0.75em;"><tr>',
                       paste(nums17, collapse = ""), "</tr><tr>", paste(cells17, collapse = ""),
                       "</tr></table></div>"))
```

  The same brackets are used inside `cor()` in section 3.1.3.

The rates are per thousand households, so a value of 500 for `TV_PR` means that half of the
households own a television. The chapter calls them penetration rates.
:::

::: callout-note
## Why the counts are turned into rates

A township with more households has more households owning a radio, whatever the level of access.
Dividing each count by the township's number of households makes the townships comparable, and
multiplying by 1,000 expresses the result per thousand households:

$$\text{penetration rate} = \frac{\text{households owning the item}}{\text{total households}} \times 1000$$
:::

The rest of the exercise is built on these penetration rates. Their distributions, maps and
correlations are examined in Part 1, five of them are used as the clustering variables, and every
set of clusters and regions on this page is formed from those five.

## Joining the ICT penetration rates to the township boundaries

As in section 12.5.2.1, the penetration rates are joined to the township polygons on the township
code.

```{r}
shan_sf <- left_join(shan_sf, ict_derived, by = c("TS_PCODE" = "TS_PCODE"))
names(shan_sf)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
The block uses one function:

```r
left_join(x, y, by = NULL)                                # dplyr
```

- `left_join()` keeps every row of `x`, the township polygons, and adds the columns of `y` from the
  row with the same township code. `by = c("TS_PCODE" = "TS_PCODE")` names the key in each table.
- The two tables have three other column names in common: `DT` (district name), `DT_PCODE` (district
  code) and `TS` (township name). `left_join()` merges only the key, so both copies of each of the
  three are kept, with a suffix for the table each copy came from: `.x` for `x` (`shan_sf`) and `.y`
  for `y` (`ict_derived`).

**The join, step by step**

The join is shown below for two townships, Mongmit and Pindaya.

`shan_sf` no longer has a column called `TS`, so the code in section 3.1.4 selects `"TS.x"`. The
join adds 16 columns after the 6 columns of `shan_sf`, so the five clustering rates, `RADIO_PR` to
`COMPUTER_PR`, are columns 17 to 21 in the list printed above, the positions used in section 3.4.
:::

The township name is the same in `TS.x` and `TS.y` for all 55 townships. The district is different
for six townships, because Myanmar reorganised some districts of Shan State in 2014 and 2015: the
census table has the districts at the time of the 2014 census, and the boundary file has the
reorganised ones. The township codes are the same in both files, so the join is not affected.

The analysis uses one township name and no district column, so there is no analytical reason to keep
both copies. The chapter's join is kept here so that the chapter's `TS.x` and `17:21` work
unchanged. Dropping the three duplicates first, with
`left_join(shan_sf, select(ict_derived, -DT_PCODE, -DT, -TS), by = "TS_PCODE")`, would leave the
name as `TS` and move the rates to columns 14 to 18.

The joined `shan_sf` is the table used for the rest of the exercise:

| Columns | Used for | Sections |
|------|---------|-----|
| `geometry` | maps; the neighbour list for SKATER, Moran's I and `rgeoda` | throughout; 3.2.1, 4.1, 4.7 |
| `TS.x` | township labels in the clustering table and in printed results | 3.1.4, 4.5, 4.8 |
| the six rates | maps, clustering variables, Moran's I, cluster profiles | 3.1, 3.4, 4.1, 4.8 |
| `TT_HOUSEHOLDS` | a map of households; a minimum number of households per region; region profiles | 3.1.2, 4.5, 4.7, 4.8 |
| `ST` | comparing the regions with the three parts of the state | 4.8 |
| `DT.x`, `DT_PCODE.x`, `DT.y`, `DT_PCODE.y`, `TS.y` | not used | |

# Part 1: Chapter 12

This part follows r4gdsa [Chapter 12](https://r4gdsa.netlify.app/chap12.html), sections 12.5 to
12.10. In section 3.1 the townships are clustered on their ICT rates alone. In sections 3.2 and 3.3,
SKATER and ClustGeo add the location of the townships to the clustering, and section 3.4 has the
profiles of the clusters.

## Hierarchical cluster analysis

This section follows sections 12.5 to 12.7 of the chapter. The clustering in it uses five of the ICT
rates, without the locations of the townships.

### Distributions

The distributions show whether a variable is skewed or has outlying townships. Both affect how far
apart townships appear in the clustering later. In section 12.5.1, the count of households with a
radio is compared with the penetration rate, first with histograms and then with boxplots.

```{r}
#| fig-height: 3
ggplot(data = ict_derived,
       aes(x = `RADIO`)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20,
                 color = "black",
                 fill = "light blue")
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
The block uses two functions:

```r
ggplot(data, aes(x))                                      # ggplot2
geom_histogram(bins, color, fill)                         # ggplot2
```

- `ggplot()` names the data, and `aes(x = RADIO)` the column drawn along the horizontal axis. The
  `+` adds a layer to the chart.
- `geom_histogram(bins = 20)` divides the range of `RADIO` into 20 equal bins and draws a bar for
  the number of townships in each. `color` sets the outline of the bars and `fill` their inside.
:::

```{r}
#| fig-height: 1.8
ggplot(data = ict_derived,
       aes(x = `RADIO`)) +
  geom_boxplot(color = "black",
               fill = "light blue")
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
- `geom_boxplot()` draws the median as the line inside the box, the middle half of the townships as
  the box, and as separate points any township more than 1.5 times the height of the box beyond it.
  Those points are the outliers.
:::

The same two charts for the penetration rate:

```{r}
#| fig-height: 3
ggplot(data = ict_derived,
       aes(x = `RADIO_PR`)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20,
                 color = "black",
                 fill = "light blue")
```

```{r}
#| fig-height: 1.8
ggplot(data = ict_derived,
       aes(x = `RADIO_PR`)) +
  geom_boxplot(color = "black",
               fill = "light blue")
```

The count is strongly right-skewed, and the boxplot marks three townships as outliers. The largest
counts belong to the townships with the most households. The rate is much closer to symmetric, with
one township, Ywangan, above 480 radios per thousand households. The chapter's question is what the
two charts reveal: the skew and the outliers in the count come mostly from township size, and
dividing by the number of households removes most of both.

The chapter then draws the six penetration rates side by side, one histogram each:

```{r}
radio <- ggplot(data = ict_derived,
                aes(x = `RADIO_PR`)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20,
                 color = "black",
                 fill = "light blue")

tv <- ggplot(data = ict_derived,
             aes(x = `TV_PR`)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20,
                 color = "black",
                 fill = "light blue")

llphone <- ggplot(data = ict_derived,
                  aes(x = `LLPHONE_PR`)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20,
                 color = "black",
                 fill = "light blue")

mphone <- ggplot(data = ict_derived,
                 aes(x = `MPHONE_PR`)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20,
                 color = "black",
                 fill = "light blue")

computer <- ggplot(data = ict_derived,
                   aes(x = `COMPUTER_PR`)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20,
                 color = "black",
                 fill = "light blue")

internet <- ggplot(data = ict_derived,
                   aes(x = `INTERNET_PR`)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20,
                 color = "black",
                 fill = "light blue")
```

```{r}
#| fig-height: 5
ggarrange(radio, tv, llphone, mphone, computer, internet,
          ncol = 3,
          nrow = 2)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
The blocks use one new function:

```r
ggarrange(..., ncol, nrow)                                # ggpubr
```

- The first block stores each histogram under a name, `radio`, `tv` and so on, without drawing it.
- `ggarrange()` draws the six stored charts together in a grid of three columns and two rows.
:::

Radio, TV and mobile phone are roughly symmetric. Land line, computer and internet are right-skewed:
most townships have few households with them, and a small number have many.

Three features of the charts are used later on this page:

| Feature of the charts | Used in |
|---------|-----------|
| The count of radios is right-skewed and the rate is close to symmetric, because larger townships have more households with every item | 2.3, the reason for using rates |
| The ranges of the rates differ widely: `r round(min(ict_derived$TV_PR))` to `r round(max(ict_derived$TV_PR))` for TV, `r round(min(ict_derived$COMPUTER_PR))` to `r round(max(ict_derived$COMPUTER_PR))` for computer | 3.1.5 and 4.2: on the raw rates, TV and mobile phone make up 81% of the squared distance between townships, and computer 0.6% |
| Ywangan has the highest radio rate, and computer, land line and internet have long right tails | 3.2.4: Ywangan is one of the two single-township SKATER regions on the raw rates. 4.5: Tachileik, Muse and Taunggyi, the three highest computer rates, are the three single-township regions on z-scores |

### Choropleth maps

Maps show where in the state the high and low values of a rate are, which the histograms of section
3.1.1 cannot show. The first map in section 12.5.2.2 is a quick map of the radio penetration rate.

```{r}
#| fig-height: 4.5
qtm(shan_sf, "RADIO_PR")
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
```r
qtm(shp, fill)                                            # tmap
```

- `qtm()` (quick thematic map) draws a choropleth map in one call, with default classes, colours and
  legend. The second argument names the column that sets the colour of each township.
:::

It then maps the number of households beside the number of households with a radio.

```{r}
#| fig-height: 4.2
TT_HOUSEHOLDS.map <- tm_shape(shan_sf) +
  tm_fill(fill = "TT_HOUSEHOLDS",
          fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(n = 5, style = "jenks"),
          fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Total households")) +
  tm_borders(col_alpha = 0.5)

RADIO.map <- tm_shape(shan_sf) +
  tm_fill(fill = "RADIO",
          fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(n = 5, style = "jenks"),
          fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Number Radio")) +
  tm_borders(col_alpha = 0.5)

tmap_arrange(TT_HOUSEHOLDS.map, RADIO.map,
             asp = NA, ncol = 2)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
The block uses six functions:

```r
tm_shape(shp)                                             # tmap
tm_fill(fill, fill.scale, fill.legend)                    # tmap
tm_scale_intervals(n, style)                              # tmap
tm_legend(title)                                          # tmap
tm_borders(col_alpha)                                     # tmap
tmap_arrange(..., asp, ncol)                              # tmap
```

- `tm_shape()` names the sf object that the layers after it draw, and each `+` adds a layer.
- `tm_fill()` colours each township by the column named in `fill`, without drawing its outline.
  `tm_borders()` draws the outlines as a separate layer, at half opacity.
- `tm_scale_intervals(n = 5, style = "jenks")` divides the values into five classes by the Jenks
  natural breaks method, which places the class boundaries where the gaps between the sorted values
  are largest.
- `tmap_arrange()` places the two stored maps side by side. `asp = NA` lets each map keep the shape
  of Shan State.

The chapter is written for tmap version 3, and the installed version is 4, which renames some
arguments. The chapter's code and the version used here:

| Chapter (tmap 3) | This page (tmap 4) |
|---|---|
| `tm_fill(col = "TT_HOUSEHOLDS", n = 5, style = "jenks", title = "Total households")` | `tm_fill(fill = "TT_HOUSEHOLDS", fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(n = 5, style = "jenks"), fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Total households"))` |
| `tm_borders(alpha = 0.5)` | `tm_borders(col_alpha = 0.5)` |

tmap 4 still accepts the chapter's version 3 code, but it translates `tm_borders(alpha = 0.5)` into
a half-transparent fill, which pales the whole map. `col_alpha` applies the transparency to the
borders, which is what the chapter intends.
:::

The chapter then draws the number of households beside the radio penetration rate, as one map with
two panels.

```{r}
#| fig-height: 4.6
tm_shape(shan_sf) +
  tm_polygons(fill = c("TT_HOUSEHOLDS", "RADIO_PR"),
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "jenks"),
              fill.free = TRUE) +
  tm_facets(ncol = 2)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
- Given two column names in `fill`, `tm_polygons()` draws one panel for each, and
  `tm_facets(ncol = 2)` places the panels side by side. `fill.free = TRUE` gives each panel its own
  classes and legend, because the two columns are on different scales.
- The chapter's version 3 code is
  `tm_polygons(c("TT_HOUSEHOLDS", "RADIO_PR"), style = "jenks") + tm_facets(sync = TRUE, ncol = 2)`.
:::

The first pair of maps shows that the count of radios follows the number of households: the
townships in the darkest class are largely the same on both maps. The chapter's question is what
differs between the two panels. The highest radio rates are along the western edge of the state,
from the north-west to the south-west, with one more township in the east. Several of the townships
with the most households, such as the darkest township in the north of the left-hand panel, have
only moderate rates. Dividing by the number of households removes the effect of township size.

Three features of the maps are used later on this page:

| Feature of the maps | Used in |
|---------|-----------|
| The map of radio counts has much the same pattern as the map of households | 2.3, the reason for using rates |
| The highest radio rates are along the western edge of the state | 4.1: radio is one of the two rates with significant spatial autocorrelation (Moran's I 0.44). 4.8: the "High radio" region of REDCAP is on the western edge, and seven of the ten highest radio rates are in it |
| Households are concentrated in a few large townships, Taunggyi the largest with 82,604 | 4.5 and 4.7: a minimum number of households per region. Taunggyi meets the minimum of 50,000 in section 4.5 on its own |

### Correlation between the variables

Two variables that are highly correlated measure much the same thing. If both enter the clustering,
that dimension is counted twice. In section 12.6, the correlations are checked before the variables
are chosen.

```{r}
#| fig-height: 6
cluster_vars.cor <- cor(ict_derived[, 12:17])
corrplot.mixed(cluster_vars.cor,
               lower = "ellipse",
               upper = "number",
               tl.pos = "lt",
               diag = "l",
               tl.col = "black")
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
The block uses two functions:

```r
cor(x)                                                    # stats
corrplot.mixed(corr, lower, upper, tl.pos, diag, tl.col)  # corrplot
```

- `cor()` returns the matrix of Pearson correlations between every pair of columns.
- `ict_derived[, 12:17]` picks part of the table. Square brackets after a table take the form
  `table[rows, columns]`. Nothing before the comma means every row, all 55 townships. `12:17` after
  the comma is the sequence 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, which means columns 12 to 17: the six
  penetration rates, as the column table in section 2.3 shows. `cor()` accepts numbers only, so the
  name and code columns (1 to 4) and the counts (5 to 11) are left out.
- `corrplot.mixed()` draws the matrix in two halves. `lower = "ellipse"` draws each correlation
  below the diagonal as an ellipse, narrower for a stronger correlation, and tilted right for a
  positive one. `upper = "number"` prints the coefficient above the diagonal. `tl.pos = "lt"` puts
  the variable names on the left and top, `diag = "l"` draws the diagonal in the style of the lower
  half, and `tl.col` sets the colour of the names.
:::

Computer and internet are correlated at 0.87, the highest pair. The chapter keeps computer and drops
internet. TV, mobile phone and computer are also correlated with each other at about 0.7. Radio is
nearly uncorrelated with the others, and is negatively correlated with land line (−0.31).

::: callout-note
## Why one of two highly correlated variables is dropped

Euclidean distance adds one squared difference for each variable. Computer and internet ownership
are high in the same townships, so a difference on one is usually a difference on the other, and the
same difference is counted twice.

```{r}
#| echo: false
nb_tmp <- poly2nb(shan_sf)
skater_groups <- \(X) {
  set.seed(1234)
  tree <- mstree(nb2listw(nb_tmp, nbcosts(nb_tmp, X), style = "B"))
  spdep::skater(tree[, 1:2], X, ncuts = 5)$groups
}
rates6 <- c("RADIO_PR", "TV_PR", "LLPHONE_PR", "MPHONE_PR", "COMPUTER_PR", "INTERNET_PR")
x6 <- st_drop_geometry(shan_sf)[, rates6]
x5 <- x6[, 1:5]
d1_tmp <- as.dist(st_distance(shan_sf, shan_sf))
ari_hc <- adjustedRandIndex(cutree(hclust(dist(x5), method = "ward.D"), 6),
                            cutree(hclust(dist(x6), method = "ward.D"), 6))
ari_sk <- adjustedRandIndex(skater_groups(x5), skater_groups(x6))
ari_cg <- adjustedRandIndex(cutree(hclustgeo(dist(x5), d1_tmp, alpha = 0.2), 6),
                            cutree(hclustgeo(dist(x6), d1_tmp, alpha = 0.2), 6))
dist_cor <- cor(dist(x5), dist(x6))
```

Each method in Part 1 was run twice on the raw rates, once without internet, as in the chapter, and
once with it. An adjusted Rand index of 1 would mean the same six clusters both times (the index is
explained in section 4.2).

| Section | Use of the Euclidean distance | Adjusted Rand index, without and with internet |
|----|-----------|-----|
| 3.1 Hierarchical clustering | the two closest clusters are merged at each step | `r round(ari_hc, 2)` |
| 3.2 SKATER | the minimum spanning tree is built from the edge costs, and each cut reduces the within-region sum of squares | `r round(ari_sk, 2)` |
| 3.3 ClustGeo, α = 0.2 | D0, the variable part of the criterion | `r round(ari_cg, 2)` |

The distances themselves change very little: the two distance matrices are correlated
at `r round(dist_cor, 4)`. The clusters change more, because they are weakly separated (section
4.4). A small change in the distances can change which two clusters are merged first, and every
later merge depends on that one. SKATER changes least, because nearly the same edges are in its
minimum spanning tree both times.

In the chapter, internet is dropped at a correlation of 0.87, and the pairs at about 0.7, such as TV
and mobile phone (0.72), are kept. No threshold is given in the chapter.
:::

### The clustering variables

The clustering functions take a plain table of numbers: one row per township and one column per
variable, with no geometry and no text columns. This step builds that table from `shan_sf`, keeps
the five rates chosen in section 3.1.3, and uses the township names as row names, so that the
dendrogram in section 3.1.10 labels each leaf with its township.

```{r}
cluster_vars <- shan_sf |>
  st_set_geometry(NULL) |>
  select("TS.x", "RADIO_PR", "TV_PR", "LLPHONE_PR", "MPHONE_PR", "COMPUTER_PR")
row.names(cluster_vars) <- cluster_vars$"TS.x"
shan_ict <- select(cluster_vars, c(2:6))
head(shan_ict, 5)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
The block uses three functions:

```r
st_set_geometry(x, NULL)                                  # sf
select(.data, ...)                                        # dplyr
row.names(x) <- value                                     # base R
```

- `st_set_geometry(NULL)` removes the geometry column, so the result is an ordinary data frame. The
  clustering functions accept only numbers.
- `select()` keeps the township name and five of the rates, leaving out `INTERNET_PR`.
- `row.names(cluster_vars) <- cluster_vars$"TS.x"` makes the township names the row labels, as the
  steps below show.
- The second `select()` keeps columns 2 to 6, dropping the name column, which is now held in the row
  names.

Three rows of the table, before and after the `row.names()` line and the second `select()` line:

The township name is no longer a column, which the clustering functions could not use, but it
remains as a label on each row, and the distance matrix and the dendrogram take their labels from
it.
:::

::: callout-note
## Why the township is the unit of analysis

Each row of `shan_ict` is one township. The township name can label the rows because no two
townships share a name. A district name is shared by several townships, so it cannot label the rows.

The township is also the most detailed level in the data. The maps show computer ownership at three
levels on one colour scale. A district or part of the state has the rate of all its households
together.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 4.2
level_rates <- \(col) shan_sf |>
  group_by(unit = .data[[col]]) |>
  summarise(rate = sum(COMPUTER) / sum(TT_HOUSEHOLDS) * 1000,
            geometry = st_union(st_buffer(geometry, 50)))
levels_sf <- list(`3 parts of the state (ST)` = level_rates("ST"),
                  `13 districts (DT.x)` = level_rates("DT.x"),
                  `55 townships (TS.x)` = level_rates("TS.x"))
rate_lims <- range(unlist(map(levels_sf, "rate")))
level_plots <- imap(levels_sf, \(g, name) ggplot(g) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = rate), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.3) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(limits = rate_lims, option = "magma", direction = -1,
                       name = "computers per\n1,000 households") +
  labs(title = name) + theme_void())
patchwork::wrap_plots(level_plots, ncol = 3, guides = "collect") &
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
tgy_ts <- levels_sf[[3]]$rate[levels_sf[[3]]$unit == "Taunggyi"]
tgy_dt <- levels_sf[[2]]$rate[levels_sf[[2]]$unit == "Taunggyi"]
```

When townships are combined into districts, the differences between them are lost: Taunggyi
township, at `r round(tgy_ts)` computers per thousand households, is in a district with a rate
of `r round(tgy_dt)`.
:::

### Standardisation

The clustering methods below measure how far apart two townships are with Euclidean distance, the
square root of the sum of squared differences across the variables. A variable with a larger spread
contributes larger squared differences. Sections 12.7.3 and 12.7.4 compute two standardised versions
of the variables.

```{r}
shan_ict.std <- normalize(shan_ict)
summary(shan_ict.std)
```

```{r}
shan_ict.z <- scale(shan_ict)
describe(shan_ict.z)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
The two blocks use three functions:

```r
normalize(x)                                              # heatmaply
scale(x, center = TRUE, scale = TRUE)                     # base R
describe(x)                                               # psych
```

- `normalize()` applies min-max scaling to each column: it subtracts the minimum and divides by the
  range, so every column runs from 0 to 1.
- `scale()` subtracts each column's mean and divides by its standard deviation, which gives z-scores
  with mean 0 and standard deviation 1. It returns a matrix.
- `describe()` prints the mean, standard deviation, median, range, skew and kurtosis of each column.
  The chapter uses it here because `summary()` does not show the standard deviation.

:::

```{r}
#| fig-height: 3.5
r <- ggplot(data = ict_derived,
            aes(x = `RADIO_PR`)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20,
                 color = "black",
                 fill = "light blue") +
  ggtitle("Raw values without standardisation")

shan_ict_s_df <- as.data.frame(shan_ict.std)
s <- ggplot(data = shan_ict_s_df,
            aes(x = `RADIO_PR`)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20,
                 color = "black",
                 fill = "light blue") +
  ggtitle("Min-Max Standardisation")

shan_ict_z_df <- as.data.frame(shan_ict.z)
z <- ggplot(data = shan_ict_z_df,
            aes(x = `RADIO_PR`)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20,
                 color = "black",
                 fill = "light blue") +
  ggtitle("Z-score Standardisation")

ggarrange(r, s, z,
          ncol = 3,
          nrow = 1)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
- The three charts are histograms of the same variable, `RADIO_PR`, on the three scales. `ggtitle()`
  adds a title above each.
- `normalize()` returns a data frame but `scale()` returns a matrix, and `ggplot()` takes a data
  frame, so `as.data.frame()` converts both before plotting.
- `ggarrange()` draws the three stored charts in one row.
:::

The chapter's question is what can be concluded from the three histograms. The shapes are identical.
Both methods are linear rescalings, which move and stretch the axis without changing the shape of
the distribution. The range changes, and so does the weight of the variable in a Euclidean distance.

The chapter then continues with the **raw** rates, `shan_ict`, for every clustering step that
follows, and the standardised versions are not used again. The effect of that decision is measured
in section 4.2.

::: callout-note
## How the scale of a variable affects its weight in the distance

The Euclidean distance between two townships adds up the squared difference on each variable. A
variable measured on a wide range produces large differences, and a variable on a narrow range
produces small ones, whatever their importance to the question.
:::

### Proximity matrix

The clustering in section 3.1.7 groups townships whose ICT rates are close. `hclust()` takes as its
input the distance between every pair of townships, and not the rates themselves, because at each
step it compares only distances, first between townships and then between clusters. Computing the
distances first, with `dist()`, sets the kind of distance separately from the clustering, and the
same distances are used again for ClustGeo in section 3.3.

```{r}
proxmat <- dist(shan_ict, method = "euclidean")
as.matrix(proxmat)[1:4, 1:4]
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
The block uses one function:

```r
dist(x, method = "euclidean")                             # stats
```

- `dist()` computes the distance between every pair of rows. With 55 townships there are 55 × 54 / 2
  = 1,485 pairs. The result is stored as the lower triangle only, in an object of class `dist`.
- `as.matrix()` converts it to a full square matrix so that a corner of it can be printed. The
  chapter prints the whole object, which is 1,485 numbers.
:::

::: callout-note
## What the Euclidean distance between two townships measures

The distance is not a distance on the map. Each township is treated as a point whose coordinates are
its rates, and the distance is the length of the straight line between two such points, in
households per thousand. With two rates the points can be drawn, and the distance is the long side
of a right-angled triangle whose other two sides are the differences in the two rates:

$$d = \sqrt{(x_2 - x_1)^2 + (y_2 - y_1)^2}$$

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 4.6
pair2 <- shan_ict[c("Mongmit", "Pindaya"), ]
x1 <- pair2$TV_PR[1]; y1 <- pair2$MPHONE_PR[1]
x2 <- pair2$TV_PR[2]; y2 <- pair2$MPHONE_PR[2]
ggplot() +
  annotate("segment", x = x1, xend = x2, y = y1, yend = y1, linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate("segment", x = x2, xend = x2, y = y1, yend = y2, linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate("segment", x = x1, xend = x2, y = y1, yend = y2, colour = "red", linewidth = 1) +
  annotate("point", x = c(x1, x2), y = c(y1, y2), colour = "red", size = 3) +
  annotate("text", x = c(x1, x2), y = c(y1, y2), label = rownames(pair2),
           hjust = c(-0.25, 1.25), size = 4) +
  annotate("text", x = (x1 + x2) / 2, y = y1 + 7, size = 3.4,
           label = sprintf("difference in TV_PR = %.1f", abs(x1 - x2))) +
  annotate("text", x = x2 - 3, y = (y1 + y2) / 2, hjust = 1, size = 3.4,
           label = sprintf("difference in\nMPHONE_PR = %.1f", abs(y1 - y2))) +
  annotate("text", x = (x1 + x2) / 2 + 6, y = (y1 + y2) / 2 - 6, hjust = 0, size = 3.4,
           colour = "red", label = sprintf("√(%.1f² + %.1f²) = %.1f",
                                           abs(x1 - x2), abs(y1 - y2),
                                           sqrt((x1 - x2)^2 + (y1 - y2)^2))) +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(x2 - 75, x1 + 55), ylim = c(y2 - 12, y1 + 15)) +
  labs(x = "TV_PR, households per thousand", y = "MPHONE_PR, households per thousand")
```

With all five rates the formula has five squared differences under the square root, one for each
rate, and the points can no longer be drawn. For Mongmit and Pindaya the five squared differences
give a distance of `r round(as.matrix(proxmat)["Mongmit", "Pindaya"], 1)`, the value printed above.
:::

### Hierarchical clustering

Agglomerative hierarchical clustering starts with every township in its own cluster and at each step
merges the two closest clusters, until one cluster remains. The methods differ in how they measure
the distance between two clusters that each contain several townships. Ward's method merges the pair
whose merger increases the total within-cluster sum of squares by the least.

```{r}
hclust_ward <- hclust(proxmat, method = "ward.D")
```

```{r}
#| fig-height: 6
plot(hclust_ward, cex = 0.6)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
The block uses two functions:

```r
hclust(d, method = "complete")                            # stats
plot(x, cex)                                              # base R, for hclust objects
```

- `hclust()` runs agglomerative clustering on a `dist` object. `method` selects the rule for the
  distance between clusters. It provides eight, among them `"ward.D"` and `"ward.D2"`, which give
  different trees on the same distances.
- `plot()` on an `hclust` object draws the dendrogram. `cex = 0.6` shrinks the township labels.
:::

::: callout-note
## How agglomerative clustering builds the tree

The procedure is easiest to follow on six points. Each point starts as its own cluster. At each step
the two clusters whose merger adds least to the within-cluster sum of squares are joined, which is
Ward's criterion, and the height of the join in the dendrogram records that increase. After five
merges one cluster remains. Cutting the tree at a chosen height gives the clusters.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 3.4
toy <- tibble(id = LETTERS[1:6], x = c(1, 1.4, 1.2, 4, 4.5, 4.2), y = c(1, 1.3, 2.1, 1.2, 1.5, 3))
toy_tree <- hclust(dist(toy[, c("x", "y")]), method = "ward.D2")
toy_tree$labels <- toy$id
toy$cluster <- factor(cutree(toy_tree, 2))

p_pts <- ggplot(toy, aes(x, y, colour = cluster)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) + geom_text(aes(label = id), nudge_x = 0.2, colour = "black") +
  coord_equal() + labs(title = "Six points, cut into two clusters") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

p_tree <- fviz_dend(toy_tree, k = 2, k_colors = scales::hue_pal()(2)[cutree(toy_tree, 2)[toy_tree$order][c(1, 6)]],
                    cex = 0.9, main = "The dendrogram and the cut",
                    ylab = "merge height") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = mean(rev(toy_tree$height)[1:2]), linetype = "dashed", colour = "red")

patchwork::wrap_plots(p_pts, p_tree)
```

The dashed line cuts the tree below its last merge and leaves two clusters, {A, B, C} and {D, E, F}.
The same procedure on the 55 townships gives the dendrogram above, and `cutree()` makes the cut in
section 3.1.12.
:::

### Choice of agglomeration method

Ward's method was used in section 3.1.7 without a comparison. The chapter chooses the method by
building a tree with each of four methods, computing the agglomerative coefficient of each tree, and
keeping the method with the highest coefficient.

```{r}
m <- c("average", "single", "complete", "ward")
names(m) <- c("average", "single", "complete", "ward")

ac <- function(x) {
  agnes(shan_ict, method = x)$ac
}

map_dbl(m, ac)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
The block uses two functions:

```r
agnes(x, method = "average")                              # cluster
map_dbl(.x, .f)                                           # purrr
```

- `m` is a vector of the four method names. The methods differ in how the distance between two
  clusters is measured: single linkage uses the closest pair of townships, complete linkage the
  farthest pair, average linkage the mean over all pairs, and Ward the increase in the
  within-cluster sum of squares. Slide 11 uses the same three linkages for REDCAP.
- `names(m) <- ...` gives each element of `m` a name, here the same text as its value. `map_dbl()`
  copies these names to its result, so each coefficient is printed under the name of its method.
- `ac <- function(x) { ... }` defines a new function called `ac`. `function(x)` means that it takes
  one input, called `x` inside the braces, and the value of the last line in the braces is what it
  returns. `ac("ward")` runs `agnes(shan_ict, method = "ward")`.
- `agnes()` runs the same kind of agglomerative clustering as `hclust()`, and computes the Euclidean
  distances from `shan_ict` itself. It returns a list, and `$ac` takes the element called `ac` from
  it, the agglomerative coefficient, in the same way as `$` takes a column from a table in section
  3.1.4.
- `map_dbl(m, ac)` calls `ac()` once for each element of `m` and collects the four numbers into one
  named vector. `dbl` stands for double, R's type for decimal numbers.

The block gives the same result as the four calls written out:

```r
c(average  = agnes(shan_ict, method = "average")$ac,
  single   = agnes(shan_ict, method = "single")$ac,
  complete = agnes(shan_ict, method = "complete")$ac,
  ward     = agnes(shan_ict, method = "ward")$ac)
```
:::

::: callout-note
## What the agglomerative coefficient measures

For each township $i$, `agnes()` computes the ratio

$$m(i) = \frac{\text{height at which township } i \text{ is first merged}}{\text{height of the final merge}}$$

and the agglomerative coefficient is the average of one minus that ratio over the $n$ townships (the
`agnes()` documentation; Kaufman and Rousseeuw, 1990):

$$\text{AC} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \bigl(1 - m(i)\bigr)$$

A township merged into its group low in the tree has $m(i)$ close to 0, and $1 - m(i)$ close to 1.

A coefficient close to 1 therefore means that most townships are in tight groups, and the groups are
joined to each other only much higher in the tree. The UC Business Analytics tutorial, the source of
this part of the chapter, calls this a strong clustering structure. A lower coefficient means that
the merges are spread through the tree, with no clear gap between groups. The two examples have six
points each:

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 5.5
ac_example <- function(x, y, title) {
  a <- agnes(data.frame(x, y, row.names = LETTERS[1:6]), method = "ward")
  pts <- ggplot(tibble(x, y, id = LETTERS[1:6]), aes(x, y, label = id)) +
    geom_point(colour = "steelblue", size = 2.5) + geom_text(nudge_y = 0.12) +
    coord_equal(ylim = c(0.5, 2)) + labs(title = title, x = NULL, y = NULL)
  tree <- fviz_dend(as.hclust(a), cex = 0.8, main = sprintf("coefficient %.2f", a$ac),
                    ylab = "merge height") +
    geom_hline(yintercept = max(a$height), linetype = "dashed", colour = "red")
  list(pts, tree)
}
ex_tight <- ac_example(c(1, 1.3, 1.1, 5, 5.2, 4.9), c(1, 1.2, 1.4, 1.1, 1.4, 1.2),
                       "Two tight groups")
ex_spread <- ac_example(c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6), c(1, 1.3, 1, 1.2, 1, 1.3), "Evenly spread")
patchwork::wrap_plots(c(ex_tight, ex_spread), ncol = 2, byrow = FALSE, heights = c(1, 1.4))
```

The dashed red line is the final merge. In the first example every point is merged into its group
far below it. In the second, the merge heights increase steadily up to it.
:::

Ward's method scores highest, 0.943, and the chapter uses Ward's method from here on.

### Number of clusters

The dendrogram can be cut into any number of clusters, k. The chapter uses the gap statistic to
choose k from the data: it compares how tightly the townships are grouped at each k with how tightly
data with no clusters would be grouped. The number chosen, six, is used for every set of clusters on
the rest of the page.

```{r}
set.seed(12345)
gap_stat <- clusGap(shan_ict,
                    FUN = hcut,
                    nstart = 25,
                    K.max = 10,
                    B = 50)
print(gap_stat, method = "firstmax")
```

```{r}
#| fig-height: 3.5
fviz_gap_stat(gap_stat)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
The two blocks use three functions:

```r
clusGap(x, FUNcluster, K.max, B, ...)                     # cluster
hcut(x, k, hc_method = "ward.D2", ...)                    # factoextra
fviz_gap_stat(gap_stat)                                   # factoextra
```

- `clusGap()` clusters the data for k = 1 to `K.max`, and for each k also clusters `B` = 50
  reference data sets generated without structure. The gap is the difference between the reference
  and observed log dispersion. `set.seed()` fixes the random reference sets so that the result
  repeats.
- `FUN = hcut` makes `clusGap()` cluster with `hcut()`, which runs hierarchical clustering and cuts
  the tree into k groups. Its default method is `"ward.D2"`. `nstart = 25` is passed on to `hcut()`,
  which does not use it, because `nstart` is an argument of k-means.
- `print(method = "firstmax")` reports the first local maximum of the gap as the recommended k.
- `fviz_gap_stat()` plots the gap for each k with an error bar, explained in the callout below. Its
  dashed line marks the k chosen by its default rule, `firstSEmax`: the smallest k whose gap is
  within one standard error of the first peak.
:::

The recommended number is 1. The chapter reads the chart as showing that "the 6-cluster gives the
largest gap statistic" and retains six clusters. In the printed table, k = 1 has the largest gap
(0.274), and the gap for k = 6 (0.222) is within 0.02 of every other value from k = 2 to 10, while
each standard error is about 0.04. This part keeps six clusters, so that the results can be compared
with the chapter. The number of clusters on this page is therefore not set by the gap statistic,
which is compared with other criteria in section 4.4.

::: callout-note
## What the gap statistic compares

$W_k$, the within-cluster dispersion, is the sum of the squared distances from each township to the
centre of its cluster when the tree is cut into $k$ clusters. It falls as $k$ rises, because more
clusters always fit the data more closely. `clusGap()` compares its fall on the data with its fall
on 50 reference data sets of the same size, spread evenly over the range of the data, which have no
clusters:

$$\text{gap}(k) = \text{average of } \log W_k \text{ over the reference sets} - \log W_k \text{ of the data}$$

The two terms are the two curves below, drawn for the Shan rates. The gap at each $k$ is the
vertical distance between them.

How to read the gap:

- **A smaller $W_k$ alone means nothing.** Adding a cluster always makes $W_k$ smaller, in the data
  and in the reference sets alike.
- **A large gap means unusually tight clusters.** The townships are much closer to the centres of
  their clusters than points with no clusters would be.
- **A rise in the gap marks real groups.** The gap rises at a $k$ where the data have groups, and
  stays flat where an extra cluster only splits the data as it would split random points.
- **The peak gives the number of clusters.** A flat gap, as for the Shan rates, gives no clear
  number.

Why each $k$ has an error bar:

- **The reference sets are random.** Each of the 50 reference data sets gives a slightly different
  $\log W_k$, so the gap is an estimate.
- **The bar is one standard error each way.** It runs from one standard error below the gap to one
  above, from the spread of the 50 reference values. The short horizontal lines mark its ends.

How to read the chart of `fviz_gap_stat()`:

- **Each point is the gap at one $k$**, and the line joins the points.
- **A long bar** means an uncertain gap.
- **Two bars that overlap** belong to gaps that are not clearly different. On the Shan chart all the
  bars overlap, so no $k$ is clearly better than another.
- **The dashed vertical line** is the $k$ chosen by the `firstSEmax` rule.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 3.2
as_tibble(gap_stat$Tab) |>
  mutate(k = row_number()) |>
  pivot_longer(c(logW, E.logW), names_to = "curve", values_to = "value") |>
  mutate(curve = recode(curve, logW = "observed, log(W)", E.logW = "reference, E[log(W)]")) |>
  ggplot(aes(k, value, colour = curve)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:10) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("steelblue", "grey50")) +
  labs(y = "log within-cluster dispersion", colour = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

On the Shan rates the two curves are almost parallel, so the gap hardly changes with $k$.

Two generic examples, of 90 points each, show the gap with and without clusters, with the same bars
as the chart of `fviz_gap_stat()` above:

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 5.5
set.seed(42)
gap_examples <- list(
  `three clear clusters` = tibble(x = c(rnorm(30, 0, 0.4), rnorm(30, 4, 0.4), rnorm(30, 2, 0.4)),
                                 y = c(rnorm(30, 0, 0.4), rnorm(30, 0, 0.4), rnorm(30, 3.5, 0.4))),
  `no clusters` = tibble(x = runif(90, -1, 5), y = runif(90, -1, 4.5)))
gap_plots <- imap(gap_examples, \(d, name) {
  g <- clusGap(as.data.frame(d), FUN = hcut, K.max = 8, B = 50)
  tab <- as_tibble(g$Tab) |> mutate(k = row_number())
  pts <- ggplot(d, aes(x, y)) + geom_point(colour = "steelblue", size = 1) + coord_equal() +
    labs(title = name, x = NULL, y = NULL)
  gp <- ggplot(tab, aes(k, gap)) + geom_line() + geom_point() +
    geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = gap - SE.sim, ymax = gap + SE.sim), width = 0.2) +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:8) + coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-0.1, 0.95)) + labs(y = "gap")
  list(pts, gp)
})
patchwork::wrap_plots(c(gap_plots[[1]], gap_plots[[2]]), ncol = 2, byrow = FALSE)
```

With three clear clusters, the gap rises sharply to a peak at $k = 3$, above the bars of its
neighbours, and the first maximum is 3. With points spread evenly, the gap is about the same at
every $k$, within the bars, and the first maximum is $k = 1$. The Shan rates in the chart above are
like the second example.
:::

### The dendrogram

The height at which two branches join is the increase in the merging criterion caused by joining
them. Two townships are similar if their branches join low in the tree. Their horizontal position is
not a measure of similarity.

```{r}
#| fig-height: 6
plot(hclust_ward, cex = 0.6)
rect.hclust(hclust_ward, k = 6, border = 1:6)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
The block uses one new function:

```r
rect.hclust(tree, k, border)                              # stats
```

- `rect.hclust()` draws a rectangle around each of the `k` groups obtained by cutting the tree.
  `border` gives the colours. The chapter passes `2:5`, four colours for six groups, so two
  rectangles reuse a colour. `1:6` gives each group its own.
:::

### Cluster heatmap

A cluster heatmap draws the data matrix as coloured cells, with the rows ordered by the dendrogram,
so that the variables on which each group is high or low can be read across.

```{r}
#| fig-height: 9
shan_ict_mat <- data.matrix(shan_ict)

heatmaply(normalize(shan_ict_mat),
          Colv = NA,
          dist_method = "euclidean",
          hclust_method = "ward.D",
          seriate = "OLO",
          colors = Blues,
          k_row = 6,
          margins = c(NA, 200, 60, NA),
          fontsize_row = 4,
          fontsize_col = 5,
          main = "Geographic Segmentation of Shan State by ICT indicators",
          xlab = "ICT Indicators",
          ylab = "Townships of Shan State")
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
The block uses two functions:

```r
data.matrix(frame)                                        # base R
heatmaply(x, Colv, dist_method, hclust_method, seriate, colors, k_row, ...)  # heatmaply
```

- `data.matrix()` converts the data frame to a numeric matrix, which `heatmaply()` requires.
- `heatmaply()` draws an interactive heatmap, in which hovering over a cell shows its township,
  variable and value. It clusters the rows itself with `dist_method` and `hclust_method`.
  `Colv = NA` leaves the columns in their original order. `seriate = "OLO"` (optimal leaf ordering)
  reorders the branches so that neighbouring rows are as similar as possible, without changing the
  tree. `k_row = 6` colours six row groups. `margins` and the font sizes set the layout.

The heatmap clusters `normalize(shan_ict_mat)`, the min-max scaled values, while the dendrogram in
section 3.1.10 and the maps in 3.1.12 use the raw values. The six groups on the heatmap are
therefore not the six groups on the map.
:::

::: callout-note
## How to read the cluster heatmap

- Each row is one township and each column one rate.
- The colour of a cell is the township's rate after min-max scaling (section 3.1.5): white for the
  lowest value in the state and dark blue for the highest.
- The rows are in the order of the dendrogram at the left of the heatmap, so rows next to each other
  are similar townships, and the six coloured branches are the six clusters.
- Reading across a row gives one township's profile. Reading down a column within one cluster shows
  whether the cluster is high or low on that rate.

Seven townships, in the same colours:

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 3.2
heat_rows <- c("Taunggyi", "Tachileik", "Muse", "Pindaya", "Ywangan", "Narphan", "Matman")
as_tibble(normalize(shan_ict_mat), rownames = "township") |>
  filter(township %in% heat_rows) |>
  pivot_longer(-township, names_to = "rate", values_to = "value") |>
  mutate(township = factor(township, levels = rev(heat_rows)),
         rate = factor(rate, levels = colnames(shan_ict_mat))) |>
  ggplot(aes(rate, township, fill = value)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", value), colour = value > 0.6), size = 3) +
  scale_fill_distiller(palette = "Blues", direction = 1, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "black", `TRUE` = "white"), guide = "none") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = "min-max\nvalue")
```

Taunggyi, Tachileik and Muse are dark on TV, mobile phone and computer. Pindaya and Ywangan are
darkest on radio. Narphan and Matman are light on almost every rate. On the full heatmap, townships
with the same pattern are in adjacent rows and form a block of similar colour.
:::

A dark cell, or a value close to 1, means the township is among the highest in the state on that
rate; a light cell, or a value close to 0, means the township is among the lowest. For example,
Tachileik's computer cell is the darkest in its column, at 1.00, because Tachileik has the highest
computer rate of the 55 townships, `r round(max(shan_ict$COMPUTER_PR))` households per thousand.

### Mapping the clusters

So far the clusters exist only as group numbers in the tree. To see where they are, each township's
group number is attached to its polygon, and the polygons are mapped by group.

```{r}
groups <- as.factor(cutree(hclust_ward, k = 6))
shan_sf_cluster <- cbind(shan_sf, as.matrix(groups)) |>
  rename(CLUSTER = as.matrix.groups.)
table(shan_sf_cluster$CLUSTER)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
The block uses three functions:

```r
cutree(tree, k)                                           # stats
cbind(...)                                                # base R, sf method
rename(.data, ...)                                        # dplyr
```

- `cutree()` cuts the tree at the height that leaves `k` groups and returns the group number of each
  township, in the row order of the data. `as.factor()` makes the numbers categories, so that the
  map draws them as categories and not as quantities.
- `cbind()` binds the group column to `shan_sf` by row position. This is correct only because
  `shan_ict` was built from `shan_sf` in the same row order. The new column is named
  `as.matrix.groups.` after the expression that produced it, and `rename()` changes the name to
  `CLUSTER`.

The same result can be written without the matrix step:
`shan_sf_cluster <- mutate(shan_sf, CLUSTER = groups)`.
:::

```{r}
#| fig-height: 5
qtm(shan_sf_cluster, "CLUSTER")
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
- `qtm()` colours each township by its cluster. `CLUSTER` holds text labels, so `qtm()` gives each
  cluster its own colour, with no order between them.
:::

The clusters are fragmented. Cluster 1 appears in the north, the centre and the south, and several
clusters are scattered across the state in small pieces. The townships in one cluster are similar in
their ICT rates, but a cluster is not one connected region. According to the chapter, the
fragmentation is the main limitation of clustering without regard to location. The six clusters are
in 24 separate pieces of territory.

## SKATER

SKATER (Spatial 'K'luster Analysis by Tree Edge Removal) was introduced by Assunção et al. (2006).
Slides 7 and 8 of the lecture and Assunção et al. (2006, sections 3.3 and 3.4) describe it in four
steps:

1. Represent the townships as nodes of a graph, with an edge between every pair of neighbours.
2. Give each edge a cost, the dissimilarity between the two townships it joins.
3. Reduce the graph to a minimum spanning tree: n − 1 edges that connect all n townships at the
   lowest total cost.
4. Remove edges from the tree. Each removal splits one branch into two, and each piece that remains
   is a region. At each step SKATER removes the edge whose removal most reduces the within-region
   sum of squares.

Because every region is a connected piece of the tree, and every edge of the tree joins two
neighbours, every region is contiguous by construction.

### Neighbour list

SKATER can only join townships that share a boundary. The neighbour list records, for each township,
the townships that touch it, and these pairs become the edges of the graph in step 1.

```{r}
shan.nb <- poly2nb(shan_sf)
summary(shan.nb)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
The block uses one function:

```r
poly2nb(pl, queen = TRUE)                                 # spdep
```

- `poly2nb()` finds, for each polygon, the polygons that share at least one boundary point with it
  (Queen contiguity, the default). The chapter first converts `shan_sf` to an sp object with
  `as_Spatial()`. The current version of `spdep` accepts sf objects directly and returns the same
  list.

The 55 townships have 264 neighbour links, 4.8 per township on average. Every township has at least
two neighbours, so no township is isolated and the graph is connected, which SKATER requires.
:::

```{r}
#| fig-height: 6
coords <- st_coordinates(st_centroid(st_geometry(shan_sf)))

plot(st_geometry(shan_sf), border = grey(0.5))
plot(shan.nb, coords, col = "blue", add = TRUE)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
The block uses four functions:

```r
st_geometry(x)                                            # sf
st_centroid(x)                                            # sf
st_coordinates(x)                                         # sf
plot(nb, coords, col, add = TRUE)                         # spdep, for nb objects
```

- `st_geometry(shan_sf)` keeps only the polygons, without the attribute columns. `st_centroid()`
  turns each polygon into one point at its centre, and `st_coordinates()` turns each point into two
  numbers, its longitude (`X`) and latitude (`Y`), one row per township. The figure after this box
  follows Mongmit through the three functions.
- The first `plot()` draws the township boundaries in grey. The second draws a line between the
  centroids of every pair of neighbours, and `add = TRUE` draws it on the same plot. The chapter
  notes that the boundaries go first, because the first call sets the extent of the plot.
:::

The three functions in the first line, applied to one township:

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 7.5
mong <- shan_sf[shan_sf$TS.x == "Mongmit", ]
mong_pt <- st_centroid(st_geometry(mong))
mong_xy <- st_coordinates(mong_pt)
arrow_panel <- function(label) {
  ggplot() +
    annotate("segment", x = 0, xend = 1, y = 0, yend = 0,
             arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.3, "cm")), linewidth = 0.8) +
    annotate("text", x = 0.5, y = 0.25, label = label, family = "mono", size = 3.2) +
    coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-0.1, 1.1), ylim = c(-0.6, 0.6), clip = "off") +
    theme_void()
}
step1 <- ggplot() + geom_sf(data = mong, fill = "grey85", colour = "grey30") +
  labs(title = "1. Mongmit's polygon") + theme_void()
step2 <- ggplot() + geom_sf(data = mong, fill = "grey92", colour = "grey60") +
  geom_sf(data = mong_pt, colour = "red", size = 3) +
  labs(title = "2. One point at its centre") + theme_void()
step3 <- ggplot() +
  annotate("text", x = 0, y = 0, hjust = 0.5, family = "mono", size = 4,
           label = sprintf("     X      Y\n%6.2f %6.2f", mong_xy[1, "X"], mong_xy[1, "Y"])) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-1, 1), ylim = c(-1, 1)) +
  labs(title = "3. Two numbers:\n   longitude, latitude") + theme_void()
nb_df <- map_dfr(seq_along(shan.nb), \(i) tibble(from = i, to = shan.nb[[i]])) |> filter(from < to)
xy_all <- as_tibble(coords) |> setNames(c("x", "y"))
step4 <- ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = shan_sf, fill = "grey95", colour = "grey75", linewidth = 0.2) +
  geom_segment(data = tibble(x = xy_all$x[nb_df$from], y = xy_all$y[nb_df$from],
                             xend = xy_all$x[nb_df$to], yend = xy_all$y[nb_df$to]),
               aes(x, y, xend = xend, yend = yend), colour = "steelblue", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_point(data = xy_all, aes(x, y), size = 0.8) +
  geom_point(aes(x = mong_xy[1, "X"], y = mong_xy[1, "Y"]), colour = "red", size = 3) +
  labs(title = "4. The same for all 55 townships: one point each, joined to its neighbours",
       subtitle = "plot(shan.nb, coords): Mongmit in red") +
  theme_void()
top <- patchwork::wrap_plots(step1, arrow_panel("st_geometry()\nst_centroid()"), step2,
                             arrow_panel("st_coordinates()"), step3,
                             widths = c(1, 0.7, 1, 0.7, 1))
patchwork::wrap_plots(top, step4, ncol = 1, heights = c(1, 1.8))
```

### Edge costs

Step 2 gives each edge a cost: the Euclidean distance of section 3.1.6 between the ICT rates of the
two townships at its ends, computed only for townships that are neighbours. Neighbours with similar
rates have a low cost. The costs are used in section 3.2.3, where the minimum spanning tree is built
from the cheapest links.

```{r}
lcosts <- nbcosts(shan.nb, shan_ict)
shan.w <- nb2listw(shan.nb, lcosts, style = "B")
summary(shan.w)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
The block uses two functions:

```r
nbcosts(nb, data, method = "euclidean")                   # spdep
nb2listw(neighbours, glist = NULL, style = "W")           # spdep
```

- `nbcosts()` computes, for every neighbour link, the same Euclidean distance as `dist()` in section
  3.1.6, on the raw rates in `shan_ict`. `dist()` computes it for all 1,485 pairs of townships;
  `nbcosts()` only for the pairs that share a boundary.
- `nb2listw()` attaches the costs to the neighbour list as weights, and the result, `shan.w`, is the
  input `mstree()` needs in section 3.2.3. `style = "B"` stores the costs unchanged. The default,
  `"W"`, would divide each township's weights by their sum so that they add up to 1, the row
  standardisation of Exercise 4, and the costs would no longer be distances. This is unrelated to
  the standardisation of the variables in section 3.1.5.

The link between Exercise 4 and this exercise is the weights object. In Exercise 4 the weight of a
link was 1, or 1 divided by the number of neighbours. Here the weight of a link is the dissimilarity
between the two townships.
:::

### Minimum spanning tree

Step 3 reduces the neighbour links to the 54 that connect all 55 townships at the lowest total cost.
