The result, the minimum spanning tree, is what SKATER cuts into regions in section 3.2.4.

```{r}
set.seed(1234)
shan.mst <- mstree(shan.w)
dim(shan.mst)
head(shan.mst)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
The block uses one function:

```r
mstree(nbw, ini = NULL)                                   # spdep
```

- `shan.w`, from section 3.2.2, is the neighbour list with the cost of each link. `mstree()` returns
  `shan.mst`, a matrix with one row for each link of the tree: the row numbers of the two townships
  in `shan_sf`, and the cost of the link.
- `mstree()` computes the minimum spanning tree of the weighted graph by Prim's algorithm: start
  from one node, and repeatedly add the cheapest edge that connects a node already in the tree to a
  node not yet in it.
- The tree has 54 rows, one fewer than the number of townships, because a tree that connects n nodes
  has n − 1 edges.
- With `ini = NULL`, the starting node is chosen at random. The tree itself does not depend on the
  start when all costs differ, but the order of its rows does, and so does the numbering of the
  SKATER groups built from it. `set.seed()` fixes the start so the page gives the same printout on
  every render. The chapter does not set a seed, so its printout starts from node 54 and this one
  from a different node.
:::

::: callout-note
## What a minimum spanning tree is

A spanning tree is a set of links that connects every point, directly or through other points,
without any loop, so there is exactly one path between any two points. With $n$ points it always has
$n - 1$ links. A graph has many spanning trees, and the minimum spanning tree is the one whose links
have the lowest total cost. The figure uses five points and seven links, with the cost on each link:

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 2.8
mst_pts <- tibble(id = c("A", "B", "C", "D", "E"), x = c(0, 2, 1, 3, 4.2), y = c(0, 0.3, 2, 2, 0.4))
mst_links <- tibble(from = c("A", "A", "B", "B", "C", "B", "D"),
                    to   = c("B", "C", "C", "D", "D", "E", "E"),
                    cost = c(4, 2, 5, 7, 3, 6, 1))
tree_panel <- function(keep, title) {
  d <- mst_links |> mutate(used = row_number() %in% keep) |>
    left_join(mst_pts, by = c(from = "id")) |>
    left_join(mst_pts, by = c(to = "id"), suffix = c("", "end"))
  ggplot(d) +
    geom_segment(aes(x, y, xend = xend, yend = yend, colour = used, linewidth = used)) +
    geom_label(aes((x + xend) / 2, (y + yend) / 2, label = cost), size = 3, fill = "white",
               label.size = 0, label.padding = unit(0.12, "lines")) +
    geom_point(data = mst_pts, aes(x, y), size = 6, shape = 21, fill = "white") +
    geom_text(data = mst_pts, aes(x, y, label = id), size = 3.2) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "steelblue", `FALSE` = "grey85"), guide = "none") +
    scale_linewidth_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = 1.3, `FALSE` = 0.5), guide = "none") +
    coord_equal(clip = "off") + theme_void() + labs(title = title) +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 10))
}
patchwork::wrap_plots(
  tree_panel(1:7, "All seven links"),
  tree_panel(c(1, 3, 4, 7), "A spanning tree, cost 4 + 5 + 7 + 1 = 17"),
  tree_panel(c(1, 2, 5, 7), "The minimum spanning tree,\ncost 4 + 2 + 3 + 1 = 10"),
  ncol = 3)
```

SKATER cuts a tree because a tree has no loops: removing any one link splits it into exactly two
connected pieces, so every cut in section 3.2.4 adds one region, and every region is contiguous. The
minimum spanning tree is made of the links between the most similar neighbours, so the links left
for cutting are between townships that are already alike, and a cut separates the most different
parts of a branch.
:::

How Prim's algorithm grows the tree is easiest to see on the same five points. The numbers on the
lines are edge costs. Starting from A, the candidates at each step are the edges that join a point
already in the tree (blue) to a point outside it (dashed), and the cheapest candidate is added
(red):

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 6.5
pts <- tibble(id = c("A", "B", "C", "D", "E"), x = c(0, 2, 1, 3, 4.2), y = c(0, 0.3, 2, 2, 0.4))
edges <- tibble(from = c("A", "A", "B", "B", "C", "B", "D"),
                to   = c("B", "C", "C", "D", "D", "E", "E"),
                cost = c(4, 2, 5, 7, 3, 6, 1))
in_tree <- "A"; tree_edges <- integer(0); frames <- list()
for (k in 1:4) {
  cand <- which(xor(edges$from %in% in_tree, edges$to %in% in_tree))
  pick <- cand[which.min(edges$cost[cand])]
  status <- rep("not yet considered", nrow(edges))
  status[cand] <- "candidate"
  status[tree_edges] <- "in the tree"
  status[pick] <- "added at this step"
  frames[[k]] <- edges |> mutate(status = status,
                                 step = paste0("Step ", k, ": add ", from[pick], "-", to[pick],
                                               " (cost ", cost[pick], ")"))
  tree_edges <- c(tree_edges, pick)
  in_tree <- union(in_tree, c(edges$from[pick], edges$to[pick]))
}
frame_df <- bind_rows(frames) |>
  left_join(pts, by = c(from = "id")) |>
  left_join(pts, by = c(to = "id"), suffix = c("", "end"))
ggplot(frame_df) +
  geom_segment(aes(x, y, xend = xend, yend = yend, colour = status, linetype = status,
                   linewidth = status)) +
  geom_label(aes((x + xend) / 2, (y + yend) / 2, label = cost), size = 3.5, fill = "white",
             label.size = 0, label.padding = unit(0.15, "lines")) +
  geom_point(data = pts, aes(x, y), size = 7, shape = 21, fill = "white") +
  geom_text(data = pts, aes(x, y, label = id)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`in the tree` = "steelblue", candidate = "orange",
                                 `added at this step` = "red", `not yet considered` = "grey80")) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c(`in the tree` = "solid", candidate = "dashed",
                                   `added at this step` = "solid", `not yet considered` = "solid")) +
  scale_linewidth_manual(values = c(`in the tree` = 1.2, candidate = 0.6,
                                    `added at this step` = 1.6, `not yet considered` = 0.4)) +
  facet_wrap(~ step, ncol = 2) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(add = 0.35)) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(add = 0.35)) +
  coord_equal(clip = "off") + theme_void() +
  labs(colour = NULL, linetype = NULL, linewidth = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
        strip.text = element_text(size = 10, hjust = 0, margin = margin(b = 6)),
        panel.spacing = unit(1.2, "lines"))
```

After four steps all five points are joined by four edges, with a total cost of 10. B was reached
last, through its cheapest link to the tree, A-B, and the more expensive links B-C, B-D and B-E were
never used. `mstree()` does the same on the 55 townships, and its output lists the 54 edges in the
order they were added, so the first row printed above is the first edge of the tree.

```{r}
#| fig-height: 6
plot(st_geometry(shan_sf), border = gray(0.5))
plot.mst(shan.mst, coords, col = "blue", cex.lab = 0.7, cex.circles = 0.005, add = TRUE)
```

Each township is now connected to the others by exactly one path. The tree keeps, from the 264
neighbour links, the 54 that join the most similar neighbours while keeping every township
connected.

### SKATER regions

Step 4 cuts the tree five times, which leaves six regions.

```{r}
clust6 <- spdep::skater(edges = shan.mst[, 1:2],
                        data = shan_ict,
                        method = "euclidean",
                        ncuts = 5)
ccs6 <- clust6$groups
table(ccs6)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
The block uses one function:

```r
spdep::skater(edges, data, ncuts, crit, vec.crit, method = "euclidean")  # spdep
```

- `edges` is the first two columns of the tree, the pairs of nodes. The costs in column 3 are not
  passed, because `skater()` recomputes the within-region sum of squares from `data` after each cut.
- `ncuts = 5` removes five edges, which leaves six regions. The argument is the number of cuts, one
  fewer than the number of regions.
- `crit` and `vec.crit` set a minimum size for each region. They are not used in the chapter.
- The `spdep::` prefix selects the `spdep` version, because `rgeoda` also has a `skater()`.

The result is a list. `$groups` holds the region of each township, and `$ssto` and `$ssw` hold the
total sum of squares and the within-region sum of squares after each cut.
:::

```{r}
round(clust6$ssw, 0)
```

The six regions have 22, 18, 11, 2, 1 and 1 townships, the sizes printed in the chapter. The first
cut reduces the within-region sum of squares from 12,613 to 10,977, and each later cut reduces it by
less. Two of the six regions are single townships, Ywangan and Narphan.

```{r}
#| fig-height: 6
plot(st_geometry(shan_sf), border = gray(0.5))
plot(clust6, coords, cex.lab = 0.7,
     groups.colors = c("red", "green", "blue", "brown", "pink", "orange"),
     cex.circles = 0.005, add = TRUE)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
- `plot()` on a `skater` object draws the pruned tree, with the edges of each region in the colour
  given for it in `groups.colors`. The chapter gives five colours for six regions, so the sixth
  region reuses the first colour. Six colours are given here.
:::

::: callout-note
## The four steps of SKATER on Shan

The two maps show steps 1 to 3 listed at the start of section 3.2: the neighbour graph with every
Queen link, and the minimum spanning tree with 54 of them.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 4
xy <- as_tibble(coords) |> setNames(c("x", "y"))
nb_edges <- map_dfr(seq_along(shan.nb), \(i) tibble(from = i, to = shan.nb[[i]])) |>
  filter(from < to)
seg <- \(e) tibble(x = xy$x[e$from], y = xy$y[e$from], xend = xy$x[e$to], yend = xy$y[e$to])
mst_edges <- tibble(from = shan.mst[, 1], to = shan.mst[, 2])

base <- ggplot() + geom_sf(data = shan_sf, fill = "grey95", colour = "grey70", linewidth = 0.2) +
  theme_void()
step_nb <- base + geom_segment(data = seg(nb_edges), aes(x, y, xend = xend, yend = yend),
                               colour = "steelblue", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_point(data = xy, aes(x, y), size = 0.7) +
  labs(title = "Steps 1-2: neighbour graph")
step_mst <- base + geom_segment(data = seg(mst_edges), aes(x, y, xend = xend, yend = yend),
                                colour = "steelblue", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_point(data = xy, aes(x, y), size = 0.7) +
  labs(title = "Step 3: minimum spanning tree")
patchwork::wrap_plots(step_nb, step_mst, ncol = 2)
```

Each dot is a township and each line an edge.

Step 4 makes the five cuts one at a time. Before each cut, the reduction in the total within-region
sum of squares is computed for the removal of every link in every current region, and the link with
the largest reduction is removed (slide 8). A cut can therefore fall in any region, and each cut
splits one region into two. The six maps show the regions before the first cut and after each cut,
with the region split at that cut in colour:

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 7
cut_groups <- cbind(1, sapply(1:5, \(k) spdep::skater(shan.mst[, 1:2], shan_ict, ncuts = k)$groups))
cut_maps <- lapply(0:5, \(k) {
  if (k == 0) {
    return(ggplot() + geom_sf(data = shan_sf, fill = "grey80", colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
             theme_void() + labs(title = "Before the first cut: 1 region of 55"))
  }
  before <- cut_groups[, k]; after <- cut_groups[, k + 1]
  split <- names(which(tapply(after, before, \(g) length(unique(g))) == 2))
  inside <- before == as.numeric(split)
  part <- ifelse(inside, paste("part", as.integer(factor(after))), "other regions")
  sizes <- sort(table(after[inside]), decreasing = TRUE)
  ggplot() +
    geom_sf(data = mutate(shan_sf, part = part), aes(fill = part), colour = "white",
            linewidth = 0.2) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = setNames(c("grey80", "#1b9e77", "#d95f02"),
                                        c("other regions", sort(unique(part[inside])))),
                      guide = "none") +
    theme_void() +
    labs(title = sprintf("Cut %d: %d townships into %d + %d", k, sum(inside), sizes[1], sizes[2]))
})
patchwork::wrap_plots(cut_maps, ncol = 3)
```

The first cut separates a band of 19 townships in the north and east from the other 36. The second
splits the 36 into 24 and 12. The last three cuts each separate one or two townships, which are the
small regions in the table in section 3.2.4.
:::

### SKATER map

The SKATER regions are attached to the polygons and mapped, beside the hierarchical clusters of
section 3.1.12, to compare the two.

```{r}
#| fig-height: 5
groups_mat <- as.matrix(clust6$groups)
shan_sf_spatialcluster <- cbind(shan_sf_cluster, as.factor(groups_mat)) |>
  rename(SP_CLUSTER = as.factor.groups_mat.)
qtm(shan_sf_spatialcluster, "SP_CLUSTER")
```

The chapter places the two maps side by side.

```{r}
#| fig-height: 5
hclust.map <- qtm(shan_sf_cluster,
                  "CLUSTER") +
  tm_borders(col_alpha = 0.5)

shclust.map <- qtm(shan_sf_spatialcluster,
                   "SP_CLUSTER") +
  tm_borders(col_alpha = 0.5)

tmap_arrange(hclust.map, shclust.map,
             asp = NA, ncol = 2)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
- `cbind()` adds the SKATER region of each township to `shan_sf_cluster` as a new column, and
  `rename()` names it `SP_CLUSTER`, as in section 3.1.12.
- The chapter writes `tm_borders(alpha = 0.5)`. The reason for `col_alpha = 0.5` under tmap 4 is
  given in section 3.1.2.
:::

The two maps show the difference on slide 5: every SKATER region is one connected piece, and the
hierarchical clusters are scattered.

## ClustGeo

ClustGeo (Chavent et al., 2018) adds a second dissimilarity, D1, measured in geographic space, to
the dissimilarity D0 in the space of the variables, and minimises a weighted combination of the two.
The weight on D1 is the mixing parameter α:

- at α = 0, only the variables count, and the result is ordinary Ward clustering;
- at α = 1, only geography counts, and the clusters are compact blocks of territory whatever their
  ICT rates;
- in between, a larger α makes the clusters more compact and less homogeneous.

The paper calls this a soft contiguity constraint. Townships that are not neighbours may still end
up in the same cluster.

### Ward-like clustering without a constraint

With α = 0, ClustGeo is ordinary Ward clustering. Running it first gives the starting point that the
geographic constraint then changes.

```{r}
#| fig-height: 6
nongeo_cluster <- hclustgeo(proxmat)
plot(nongeo_cluster, cex = 0.5)
rect.hclust(nongeo_cluster, k = 6, border = 1:6)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
The block uses one function:

```r
hclustgeo(D0, D1 = NULL, alpha = 0, scale = TRUE, wt = NULL)  # ClustGeo
```

- With only `D0`, `hclustgeo()` runs Ward-like clustering on that matrix. `D0` must be a `dist`
  object.
- According to Chavent et al. (2018, section 2.2), `hclustgeo()` is a wrapper of
  `hclust(method = "ward.D")` applied to the squared dissimilarities divided by 2n. The chapter
  describes it as the same as the `hclust()` call of section 3.1.7. The two produce different trees,
  because `ward.D` is applied to unsquared distances in section 3.1.7.
:::

```{r}
#| fig-height: 5
groups <- as.factor(cutree(nongeo_cluster, k = 6))
shan_sf_ngeo_cluster <- cbind(shan_sf, as.matrix(groups)) |>
  rename(CLUSTER = as.matrix.groups.)
qtm(shan_sf_ngeo_cluster, "CLUSTER")
```

The map is as fragmented as the map in section 3.1.12, and the cluster sizes differ from
it: `r paste(sort(table(shan_sf_ngeo_cluster$CLUSTER), decreasing = TRUE), collapse = ", ")` here
against `r paste(sort(table(shan_sf_cluster$CLUSTER), decreasing = TRUE), collapse = ", ")` there.

### Geographic distances and the choice of α

ClustGeo needs a second matrix, D1, of geographic dissimilarities, and a value of α. `st_distance()`
supplies D1, and `choicealpha()` measures, for each α, how much homogeneity in the ICT rates is
given up for how much geographic homogeneity.

```{r}
dist <- st_distance(shan_sf, shan_sf)
distmat <- as.dist(dist)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
The block uses two functions:

```r
st_distance(x, y)                                         # sf
as.dist(m)                                                # stats
```

- `st_distance()` returns the matrix of distances between every pair of features. For polygons, the
  distance is the shortest distance between their boundaries. For longitude and latitude it is
  computed on the sphere, in metres.
- `as.dist()` converts the square matrix to a `dist` object, as `hclustgeo()` requires.
- The chapter names the object `dist`, the same name as the function `dist()`. R still finds the
  function when it is called, because it looks for a function by that name, but the name is easy to
  misread.

A township and its neighbour touch, so the shortest distance between them is zero.
:::

```{r}
#| fig-height: 4.5
cr <- choicealpha(proxmat, distmat, range.alpha = seq(0, 1, 0.1), K = 6, graph = TRUE)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
The block uses one function:

```r
choicealpha(D0, D1, range.alpha, K, wt = NULL, scale = TRUE, graph = TRUE)  # ClustGeo
```

- `choicealpha()` builds the partition into `K` clusters for each α in `range.alpha`, and measures
  for each partition the proportion of the total pseudo-inertia (a generalised sum of squares)
  explained in D0 space and in D1 space. `graph = TRUE` draws both, first as the raw proportions, Q,
  then as proportions of their own maximum, Qnorm.
:::

```{r}
round(cbind(cr$Q, cr$Qnorm), 3)
```

The chapter uses α = 0.2, read from the charts. Slide 15 of the lecture gives the reasoning with
numbers from this data set: at α = 0 the partition explains 0.76 of the ICT variation, and at α = 1
the geographic partition explains 0.94 of the geographic variation. At α = 0.2 the ICT proportion
falls by 0.11 to 0.65 and the geographic proportion rises by 0.49 to 0.63. The table printed above
gives the same values.

::: callout-note
## How to read the `choicealpha()` charts

Both charts have α on the horizontal axis and one line for each matrix:

- The black line, Q0, is the share of the variation in the ICT rates (D0) that the six clusters
  explain. It is highest at α = 0, where only the rates count, and falls as α rises.
- The red dashed line, Q1, is the share of the geographic variation (D1) that the six clusters
  explain. It is lowest at α = 0 and rises with α.

Each share is one minus the within-cluster sum of squared dissimilarities divided by the total, the
quantity that `choicealpha()` calls the proportion of explained pseudo-inertia:

$$Q = 1 - \frac{\text{within-cluster sum of squared dissimilarities}}{\text{total sum of squared dissimilarities}}$$

The share of variation explained in Part 2 is the same quantity, computed on the z-scores.

The first chart draws Q0 and Q1 themselves. The second, Qnorm, divides each line by its own maximum,
so both lines start from 1 and the two losses can be compared directly. A useful α is one where Q1
has risen a long way while Q0 has fallen only a little. The printed table has the four lines as
columns, Q0, Q1, Q0norm and Q1norm, with one row for each α.
:::

### ClustGeo regions

With α chosen, the tree is built again from both matrices and cut into six clusters.

```{r}
#| fig-height: 5
clustG <- hclustgeo(proxmat, distmat, alpha = 0.2)
groups <- as.factor(cutree(clustG, k = 6))
shan_sf_Gcluster <- cbind(shan_sf, as.matrix(groups)) |>
  rename(CLUSTER = as.matrix.groups.)
qtm(shan_sf_Gcluster, "CLUSTER")
```

The clusters are more compact than at α = 0, and several of them are still split. Cluster 4 in this
printout, for instance, has townships in the north-west and in the north, a strip in the south-west,
and one township in the south-east. The split follows from the soft constraint of Chavent et al.
(2018): geography has a weight in the criterion, and a split is still allowed.

::: callout-note
## What the mixing parameter α does

The four maps cut the ClustGeo tree into six clusters at four values of α, with the chapter's two
matrices. At α = 0 the clusters are the same as those of section 3.3.1. As α rises, geography has
more weight: the clusters become compact, and at α = 1 they are six blocks of territory formed from
distance alone, whatever the ICT rates.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 7
alpha_maps <- map(c(0, 0.2, 0.5, 1), \(a) {
  g <- cutree(hclustgeo(proxmat, distmat, alpha = a), 6)
  ggplot() + geom_sf(data = mutate(shan_sf, g = factor(g)), aes(fill = g),
                     colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
    scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2", guide = "none") + theme_void() +
    labs(title = paste0("alpha = ", a))
})
patchwork::wrap_plots(alpha_maps, ncol = 2)
```
:::

## Cluster profiles

In section 12.10, the clusters are described by their ICT rates. The chapter profiles the
non-spatial `hclustgeo()` clusters of section 3.3.1, and the same clusters are profiled here. The
same profile for a set of contiguous regions is in section 4.8.

```{r}
#| fig-height: 3.5
ggplot(data = shan_sf_ngeo_cluster, aes(x = CLUSTER, y = RADIO_PR)) +
  geom_boxplot()
```

Each box is the spread of the radio rate across the townships of one cluster, and the line inside it
is the median. By median, the clusters
rank `r paste(names(sort(tapply(shan_sf_ngeo_cluster$RADIO_PR, shan_sf_ngeo_cluster$CLUSTER, median), decreasing = TRUE)), collapse = ", ")`
on radio, the order in the chapter. The chapter calls it the order of the mean, which a boxplot does
not show: by mean, the order
is `r paste(names(sort(tapply(shan_sf_ngeo_cluster$RADIO_PR, shan_sf_ngeo_cluster$CLUSTER, mean), decreasing = TRUE)), collapse = ", ")`
(the table of means below).

```{r}
#| fig-height: 5
ggparcoord(data = shan_sf_ngeo_cluster,
           columns = c(17:21),
           scale = "globalminmax",
           alphaLines = 0.2,
           boxplot = TRUE,
           title = "Multiple Parallel Coordinates Plots of ICT Variables by Cluster") +
  facet_grid(~ CLUSTER) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30))
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
The two blocks use three new functions:

```r
geom_boxplot()                                            # ggplot2
ggparcoord(data, columns, scale, alphaLines, boxplot, title)  # GGally
facet_grid(rows ~ cols)                                   # ggplot2
```


- `columns = c(17:21)` selects the five rates by position. In `shan_sf_ngeo_cluster`, columns 17 to
  21 are `RADIO_PR` to `COMPUTER_PR`, as `names(shan_sf)` printed in section 2.4 shows.
- `scale = "globalminmax"` draws every variable on one common axis without rescaling. Variables with
  larger values, TV and mobile phone, take up most of the height, and computer is compressed near
  zero, which reflects the same difference in scale described in section 3.1.5. `alphaLines = 0.2`
  makes the lines transparent, and `boxplot = TRUE` adds a boxplot on each axis.
- `facet_grid(~ CLUSTER)` draws one panel per cluster.
:::

::: callout-note
## How to read the parallel coordinate plot

A parallel coordinate plot draws each township as one line. The five rates are five vertical axes
side by side, all on the same scale, and a township's line crosses each axis at the height of its
rate. Three townships:

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 3.4
pc_rows <- c("Taunggyi", "Pindaya", "Matman")
as_tibble(shan_ict, rownames = "township") |>
  filter(township %in% pc_rows) |>
  pivot_longer(-township, names_to = "rate", values_to = "value") |>
  mutate(rate = factor(rate, levels = names(shan_ict)),
         township = factor(township, levels = pc_rows)) |>
  ggplot(aes(rate, value, group = township, colour = township)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1:5, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) + geom_point(size = 2) +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(aes(label = round(value)), size = 3, direction = "y", nudge_x = 0.15,
                           hjust = 0, segment.colour = NA, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Dark2") +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.05, 0.1))) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "households per thousand", colour = NULL)
```

Taunggyi's line is high on TV and mobile phone. Pindaya's line is highest on radio and low on mobile
phone. Matman's line is low on every axis. Townships with similar rates have lines of similar shape.

The plot above draws all 55 townships this way, one panel per cluster, with three additions:

- The lines are transparent, so a dark band is a place where many lines overlap.
- Each axis has a boxplot of the townships in the cluster: the thick line is the median, the box the
  middle half of the townships, and a dot a township far from the rest of its cluster.
- Every panel has the same vertical scale, so the boxes on one axis can be compared across panels by
  their height.

The boxes from left to right give the typical profile of a cluster, and one axis compared across the
panels shows which cluster is high or low on that rate. In panel 4, the TV and mobile phone boxes
are the highest of all six panels, with medians
of `r round(median(shan_sf_ngeo_cluster$TV_PR[shan_sf_ngeo_cluster$CLUSTER == "4"]))`
and `r round(median(shan_sf_ngeo_cluster$MPHONE_PR[shan_sf_ngeo_cluster$CLUSTER == "4"]))`
households per thousand. In panel 5, every box is near the bottom of the scale.
:::

```{r}
shan_sf_ngeo_cluster |>
  st_set_geometry(NULL) |>
  group_by(CLUSTER) |>
  summarise(n = n(),
            mean_RADIO_PR = mean(RADIO_PR),
            mean_TV_PR = mean(TV_PR),
            mean_LLPHONE_PR = mean(LLPHONE_PR),
            mean_MPHONE_PR = mean(MPHONE_PR),
            mean_COMPUTER_PR = mean(COMPUTER_PR)) |>
  kable(digits = 1)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
- `group_by()` splits the table by cluster, and `summarise()` computes one row per cluster: the
  count and the mean of each rate. `kable(digits = 1)` prints the table rounded to one decimal.
:::

Cluster numbers are arbitrary labels, so the chapter's reading of "cluster 4" holds only where the
numbering is the same as in the chapter. In this run it is: cluster 4 is a group of six townships
with the highest TV, land line, mobile phone and computer rates. The chapter describes cluster 5 as
owning "the lowest of all the five ICT". According to the means, that holds for TV, mobile phone and
computer only: cluster 6 has lower radio ownership than cluster 5, and cluster 2 lower land line
ownership.

# Part 2: Review and extension

Part 1 reproduced chapter 12. This part examines the choices in its method, and adds the methods on
the Lesson 6 slides that the chapter does not cover.

| Section | What I do | Source |
|----|--------------------------------------|------------|
| | **Checking the chapter's method** | |
| 4.1 | Test each clustering variable for spatial autocorrelation | de Souza and Taconeli (2022); Lesson 5 |
| 4.2 | Measure how much each variable weighs in the distance, and cluster on standardised values | chapter 12.7.2 to 12.7.5; Assunção et al. (2006); Rovan and Sambt (2003); UC-R tutorial |
| 4.3 | Compare `ward.D` with `ward.D2` | Chavent et al. (2018), section 2.2; UC-R tutorial |
| 4.4 | Examine the evidence for six clusters | chapter 12.7.9; UC-R tutorial; de Souza and Taconeli (2022); Rovan and Sambt (2003); Demeter and Brătucu (2013); Brown and Watson (2012) |
| 4.5 | Explain the single-township SKATER regions and set a minimum number of households | Assunção et al. (2006), section 4 |
| 4.6 | Test the geographic matrix D1 used for ClustGeo | Chavent et al. (2018), sections 4.3 and 4.4; Jaya et al. (2019) |
| | **Adding what the chapter leaves out** | |
| 4.7 | Run REDCAP, AZP and max-p, and SCHC from `rgeoda` | slides 2 and 10 to 12 |
| 4.8 | Compare all the regionalisations on homogeneity and contiguity, and profile the chosen one | slides 4 and 5; de Souza and Taconeli (2022); Brown and Watson (2012) |

Two measures are used to compare the sets of clusters in Part 2:

$$\text{share explained} = 1 - \frac{\text{within-cluster sum of squares}}{\text{total sum of squares}}$$

| Measure | What it is | How to read it | Source |
|----|-----|-----|---------|
| **Share of variation explained** | the formula above, on the standardised variables | 0: the clusters explain nothing. 1: every cluster is internally identical | Assunção et al. (2006, equation 2), as the within-region sum of squares, the `$ssw` of `skater()` in section 3.2.4. Chavent et al. (2018) and de Souza and Taconeli (2022), as the proportion of explained inertia, Q0 on slide 15 (the same number with Euclidean distances and equal weights). `rgeoda`, as "the ratio of between to total sum of squares" |
| **Number of pieces** | the count of separate connected pieces of territory that the clusters are in | 6 for six contiguous regions; more pieces, more fragmented clusters | added on this page, and not used in the readings. It measures the contiguity of slides 3 and 5, with `n.comp.nb()` from `spdep` |

```{r}
cluster_map <- function(data, var = "CLUSTER", title = NULL) {
  tm_shape(data) +
    tm_polygons(fill = var,
                fill.scale = tm_scale_categorical(values = "brewer.set2"),
                fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Cluster")) +
    tm_title(title)
}

ss_ratio <- function(X, groups) {
  X <- as.matrix(X)
  total <- sum(scale(X, scale = FALSE)^2)
  within <- sum(sapply(split(as.data.frame(X), groups),
                       \(d) sum(scale(as.matrix(d), scale = FALSE)^2)))
  1 - within / total
}

count_pieces <- function(groups, nb = shan.nb) {
  sum(sapply(unique(groups), \(g) {
    if (sum(groups == g) == 1) return(1)
    n.comp.nb(subset(nb, groups == g))$nc
  }))
}

c(explained = ss_ratio(shan_ict.z, shan_sf_cluster$CLUSTER),
  pieces = count_pieces(shan_sf_cluster$CLUSTER))
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
The block defines three functions, using these:

```r
tm_scale_categorical(values)                              # tmap
tm_title(text)                                            # tmap
scale(x, center = TRUE, scale = FALSE)                    # base R
split(x, f)                                               # base R
subset(x, subset)                                         # spdep, for nb objects
n.comp.nb(nb.obj)                                         # spdep
```

- `cluster_map()` draws a map of cluster labels with a fixed categorical palette and a title. Part 2
  has many sets of clusters, and the function draws all their maps in one format.
- `ss_ratio()`: `scale(X, scale = FALSE)` subtracts each column mean, so the sum of the squared
  result is the total sum of squares. `split()` divides the rows by cluster, and the same sum
  computed within each cluster gives the within-cluster sum of squares. The ratio is one minus their
  quotient.
- `count_pieces()`: for each cluster, `subset()` keeps only the neighbour links between townships in
  that cluster, and `n.comp.nb()` counts the connected components of what remains. A single township
  is one piece. The sum over clusters is the number of pieces.

For the hierarchical clusters of section 3.1.12, the six clusters explain 61% of the standardised
variation and are in 24 pieces.
:::

## Spatial autocorrelation of the clustering variables

SKATER and ClustGeo in sections 3.2 and 3.3 apply a spatial constraint to all five rates at once,
and the chapter attributes the fragmented map of section 3.1.12 to clustering without regard to
location. Part 1 does not test whether the rates themselves are spatially patterned. If a variable
varies across the state without regard to location, a contiguity constraint can only group townships
that differ on it.

De Souza and Taconeli (2022) apply Moran's I to each of their six educational indicators before
clustering, and report significant spatial autocorrelation for all six, which is their ground for
using spatial algorithms at all. The test is the permutation test of Lesson 5, on Queen contiguity
with row-standardised weights. The question here is which of the six ICT rates are spatially
autocorrelated.

```{r}
set.seed(1234)
lw_shan <- nb2listw(shan.nb, style = "W")
rates <- c("RADIO_PR", "TV_PR", "LLPHONE_PR", "MPHONE_PR", "COMPUTER_PR", "INTERNET_PR")

moran_by_rate <- map_dfr(rates, \(v) {
  m <- moran.mc(shan_sf[[v]], lw_shan, nsim = 999)
  tibble(rate = v, moran_I = unname(m$statistic), p_value = m$p.value)
})
kable(moran_by_rate, digits = 3)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
```r
nb2listw(neighbours, style = "W")                         # spdep
moran.mc(x, listw, nsim)                                  # spdep
map_dfr(.x, .f)                                           # purrr
```

- `nb2listw(style = "W")` turns the Queen neighbour list of section 3.2.1 into row-standardised
  weights, as in Exercise 5.
- `moran.mc()` computes Moran's I and compares it with 999 values obtained by permuting the rates
  across townships. The p-value is the rank of the observed value among the 1,000.
- `map_dfr()` runs the test once for each rate and stacks the six one-row tables.
:::

Only two rates are significantly autocorrelated at the 5% level: radio (I = 0.44) and land line (I =
0.38). Mobile phone is borderline (p = 0.055), and TV, computer and internet show no spatial pattern
that can be distinguished from a random arrangement of the same values.

Unlike de Souza and Taconeli's indicators, then, most of the ICT rates are not spatially structured.
TV and mobile phone, the two variables with the most weight in the raw distances (section 4.2), are
among those without spatial pattern, which is consistent with the fragmented map of section 3.1.12.
A regionalisation of these data can also be expected to give up a substantial share of homogeneity,
because under the constraint, neighbouring townships share a region even where their TV, mobile
phone and computer rates are unrelated.

## Scale of the clustering variables

Two standardised versions of the variables were computed in section 3.1.5, and the raw rates were
used for every clustering step after it. The chapter's own reason for standardising, in section
12.7.2, is to avoid a result "biased to clustering variables with large values". The course's own
sources all include the step. The UC Business Analytics tutorial linked under "All About R", from
which chapter sections 12.7.8 to 12.7.10 are taken, says that "the data must be standardized (i.e.,
scaled) to make variables comparable" and applies `scale()` before `dist()`. Assunção et al. (2006,
section 3.2) define the SKATER edge cost for attributes with "comparable scales, such as when they
are measured in standard deviation units", and both Rovan and Sambt (2003) and de Souza and Taconeli
(2022) standardise every variable before clustering. The bias that the omission introduces is
measured below, and the clustering is repeated on standardised variables.

Euclidean distance adds up squared differences. Summed over all pairs of townships, the squared
differences on one variable are proportional to its variance. The share of each variable in the
total is therefore its share of the summed variance.

```{r}
#| fig-height: 3.5
share <- tibble(variable = names(shan_ict),
                `Raw rates` = sapply(shan_ict, var) / sum(sapply(shan_ict, var)),
                `Min-max` = apply(shan_ict.std, 2, var) / sum(apply(shan_ict.std, 2, var)),
                `z-score` = 1 / 5) |>
  pivot_longer(-variable, names_to = "scale", values_to = "share")

ggplot(share, aes(x = share, y = variable)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  facet_wrap(~ scale) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "share of the squared Euclidean distance", y = NULL)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
- `sapply(shan_ict, var)` computes the variance of each column. Dividing by the sum gives each
  variable's share. For z-scores every variance is 1, so every share is one fifth.
- `pivot_longer()` reshapes the three share columns into rows, one row per variable and scale, which
  `facet_wrap()` needs to draw one panel per scale.
:::

```{r}
round(100 * sapply(shan_ict, var) / sum(sapply(shan_ict, var)), 1)
```

On the raw rates, mobile phone and TV together make up 81% of the distance between townships, and
computer 0.6%. The six hierarchical clusters of section 3.1 are therefore mostly a grouping on two
variables.

- Internet was removed in section 12.6 because it is correlated with computer at 0.87. On the raw
  scale, computer itself has almost no weight in the distance, so dropping internet changes the
  distances very little, although the weakly separated clusters still change (section 3.1.3).
- Land line (2.4%) has little weight either, although it is the variable on which three adjacent
  townships in Shan (North) differ most from the rest (section 4.8).
- Radio and land line, the only two rates with significant spatial autocorrelation in section 4.1,
  together account for 18% of the raw distance. On the raw scale the clustering is driven by the
  variables with the least spatial pattern.

After min-max scaling the five shares lie between 18% and 24%, and after z-scores they are equal.
The clustering is repeated on z-scores below. The Ward method used is `ward.D2`, for the reason
given in section 4.3.

```{r}
#| fig-height: 5
h_raw <- cutree(hclust(dist(shan_ict), method = "ward.D2"), k = 6)
h_z <- cutree(hclust(dist(shan_ict.z), method = "ward.D2"), k = 6)
h_mm <- cutree(hclust(dist(shan_ict.std), method = "ward.D2"), k = 6)

tibble(comparison = c("raw against z-score", "raw against min-max", "z-score against min-max"),
       ARI = c(adjustedRandIndex(h_raw, h_z), adjustedRandIndex(h_raw, h_mm),
               adjustedRandIndex(h_z, h_mm))) |>
  kable(digits = 2)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
```r
adjustedRandIndex(x, y)                                   # mclust
```

- `adjustedRandIndex()` takes two vectors of cluster labels for the same townships and returns the
  adjusted Rand index.
:::

::: callout-note
## What the adjusted Rand index measures

The adjusted Rand index compares two clusterings of the same townships. It is computed over every
pair of townships. A pair is a match when the two townships are in the same cluster in both
clusterings, or in different clusters in both. The share of pairs that match is the Rand index. The
adjusted index subtracts the share of matches expected between two random clusterings with the same
cluster sizes and rescales the result, so that it is 1 for identical clusterings and close to 0 for
clusterings that match no better than chance.

Six townships, A to F, in three clusterings:

| | A | B | C | D | E | F |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Clustering 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 2 | 2 | 2 |
| Clustering 2 | 2 | 2 | 2 | 1 | 1 | 1 |
| Clustering 3 | 1 | 1 | 2 | 2 | 2 | 2 |

- Clustering 2 has the same two groups as clustering 1, with the numbers swapped. All 15 pairs
  match, and the index is `r adjustedRandIndex(c(1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2), c(2, 2, 2, 1, 1, 1))`. The
  numbers used as labels make no difference.
- In clustering 3, C is in the other group. Ten of the 15 pairs still match, a Rand index of 0.67.
  Two random clusterings with these cluster sizes would also match on many pairs, and the adjusted
  index is `r round(adjustedRandIndex(c(1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2), c(1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 2)), 2)`.
:::

```{r}
#| fig-height: 5
tmap_arrange(
  cluster_map(mutate(shan_sf, CLUSTER = factor(h_raw)), title = "Raw rates"),
  cluster_map(mutate(shan_sf, CLUSTER = factor(h_z)), title = "z-scores"),
  ncol = 2)
```

The raw and z-score clusterings have an adjusted Rand index
of `r round(adjustedRandIndex(h_raw, h_z), 2)`. Standardisation changes the grouping substantially.
The choice between the two standardisations matters much less: z-score and min-max give almost the
same clusters (index `r round(adjustedRandIndex(h_z, h_mm), 2)`).

In section 12.7.4, the chapter warns that z-score standardisation "should only be used if we would
assume all variables come from some normal distribution". The warning does not hold:

- A z-score is a linear rescaling and assumes nothing about the shape of the distribution. The three
  histograms in section 3.1.5 have the same shape.
- Rovan and Sambt (2003, section 3) standardise all eight of their variables before Ward clustering,
  and note that "the method employed in this study does not make any distributional assumptions, so
  no other transformation of the data has been performed".

The two methods differ for an extreme township:

| | z-score | min-max |
|---|---|---|
| The largest value becomes | its distance from the mean, in standard deviations | 1 |
| An extreme township | moves the mean and the standard deviation | sets the scale of the whole variable on its own |
| Used in | the UC Business Analytics tutorial; Rovan and Sambt (2003) | de Souza and Taconeli (2022) |

Z-scores are used in the rest of Part 2.

## Ward's criterion: ward.D and ward.D2

Ward's method merges, at each step, the two clusters whose union increases the within-cluster sum of
squares by the least. The criterion is defined on squared distances, and `hclust()` has two options
for it. The chapter uses `ward.D` in section 3.1.7. With the ordinary Euclidean distances in
`proxmat`, only `ward.D2` is Ward's method:

| Call | What it does with the Euclidean distances in `proxmat` | Ward's method? |
|-------|--------------------------------------|------|
| `hclust(method = "ward.D")`, section 3.1.7 | applies Ward's merging rule to the distances as given, without squaring them | no |
| `hclust(method = "ward.D2")` | squares the distances first, then applies the rule | yes |
| `agnes(method = "ward")`, section 3.1.8 | builds the same tree as `ward.D2`, with the same merge heights | yes |
| `hclustgeo(proxmat)`, section 3.3.1 | runs `ward.D` on the squared distances divided by 2n (Chavent et al., 2018, section 2.2) | yes |

The six clusters from each call, compared with `ward.D2`:

```{r}
tree_D <- hclust(proxmat, method = "ward.D")
tree_D2 <- hclust(proxmat, method = "ward.D2")
tree_agnes <- as.hclust(agnes(shan_ict, method = "ward"))
tree_geo <- hclustgeo(proxmat)

six <- lapply(list(`ward.D` = tree_D, `ward.D2` = tree_D2, `agnes(ward)` = tree_agnes,
                   hclustgeo = tree_geo), cutree, k = 6)
tibble(call = names(six),
       `cluster sizes` = sapply(six, \(g) paste(sort(table(g), decreasing = TRUE), collapse = ", ")),
       `adjusted Rand index with ward.D2` = sapply(six, adjustedRandIndex, six$ward.D2)) |>
  kable(digits = 2)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
- `as.hclust()` converts the `agnes()` tree to the same class as the other three, so that `cutree()`
  works on all four.
- `lapply()` cuts each tree into six clusters. `sapply()` then gives, for each call, the cluster
  sizes and the adjusted Rand index with the `ward.D2` clusters (section 4.2), which is 1 for the
  same six clusters.
:::

What this means:

- **The chapter's six clusters are not Ward clusters.** The map in section 3.1.12 is of the `ward.D`
  tree, whose cluster sizes differ from those of Ward's method.
- **The agglomerative coefficient belongs to a different tree.** The 0.943 that the chapter uses to
  choose Ward is computed by `agnes()`, so it is the coefficient of the `ward.D2` tree. The map in
  section 3.1.12 is of the `ward.D` tree.
- **`hclustgeo()` is Ward's method.** Its clusters in section 3.3.1 differ from those of section
  3.1.7 because it is `ward.D2` underneath, on the same distances.
- **Part 2 uses `ward.D2`**, as does the UC Business Analytics tutorial, the source of chapter
  sections 12.7.8 to 12.7.10.

## Number of clusters

The gap statistic in section 3.1.9 has its first maximum at one cluster, and the chapter retained
six. A number of clusters can be chosen from the data, by a statistic that compares the fit for each
k, or by the purpose of the analysis, for instance a planning agency that manages six regions. The
question here is whether six clusters can be justified from the standardised variables of section
4.2.

The criteria computed below are:

- the **gap statistic**, with the "one standard error" rule of Tibshirani et al., which picks the
  smallest k whose gap is within one standard error of the best;
- the **average silhouette width**, which for each township compares its average distance to its own
  cluster with its average distance to the nearest other cluster, and ranges from −1 to 1. It is one
  of the three methods listed in chapter section 12.7.9, where only the gap statistic is computed,
  and the UC Business Analytics tutorial computes it with `fviz_nbclust(method = "silhouette")`;
- the **NbClust** majority vote over its indices. The chapter loads `NbClust` and does not run it.
  De Souza and Taconeli (2022, section 3.3) choose their number of clusters this way, from 23
  criteria.

The one-standard-error rule and the silhouette threshold of 0.25 used below come from the
cluster-analysis literature (Tibshirani et al., 2001; Kaufman and Rousseeuw, 1990) and are not part
of the course material.

```{r}
set.seed(12345)
gap_z <- clusGap(shan_ict.z, FUN = hcut, K.max = 10, B = 50)
tab <- gap_z$Tab
c(Tibs2001SEmax = maxSE(tab[, "gap"], tab[, "SE.sim"], method = "Tibs2001SEmax"),
  firstmax = maxSE(tab[, "gap"], tab[, "SE.sim"], method = "firstmax"),
  globalmax = maxSE(tab[, "gap"], tab[, "SE.sim"], method = "globalmax"))
```

```{r}
#| fig-height: 3.2
tree_z <- hclust(dist(shan_ict.z), method = "ward.D2")
sil <- sapply(2:10, \(k) mean(silhouette(cutree(tree_z, k), dist(shan_ict.z))[, "sil_width"]))

tibble(k = 2:10, silhouette = sil) |>
  ggplot(aes(k, silhouette)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 2:10) +
  labs(y = "average silhouette width")
```

```{r}
#| results: hide
#| fig-show: hide
nb_z <- NbClust(shan_ict.z, distance = "euclidean", min.nc = 2, max.nc = 10,
                method = "ward.D2", index = "all")
```

```{r}
table(nb_z$Best.nc["Number_clusters", ])
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
The blocks use three functions:

```r
maxSE(f, SE.f, method)                                    # cluster
silhouette(x, dist)                                       # cluster
NbClust(data, distance, min.nc, max.nc, method, index)    # NbClust
```

- `maxSE()` applies a rule to the column of gaps and their standard errors and returns the chosen k.
  The three rules differ in how values close to the maximum are counted.
- `silhouette()` takes the cluster labels and the distance matrix and returns the silhouette width
  of each township. The mean over townships is computed for each k from 2 to 10.
- `NbClust()` computes up to 30 indices for each k and reports the k that scores best on each index.
  `index = "all"` runs them all. It prints a long commentary and draws charts, which the chunk
  options `results: hide` and `fig-show: hide` suppress. `Best.nc` holds the k chosen by each index,
  and `table()` counts the votes.
:::

::: callout-note
## What the silhouette width measures

For one township, a is its average distance to the other townships in its own cluster, and b is its
average distance to the townships of the nearest other cluster. The silhouette width is (b − a) /
max(a, b). It is close to 1 when the township is well inside its cluster, close to 0 when it is on
the border between two clusters, and negative when it is closer to another cluster than to its own.
The average over all townships summarises the whole partition.

The figure shows the widths of the 55 townships for six clusters on the z-scores, grouped by
cluster. Many are close to zero, and some are negative.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 3.4
fviz_silhouette(silhouette(cutree(tree_z, 6), dist(shan_ict.z)), print.summary = FALSE) +
  labs(title = NULL) + theme(axis.text.x = element_blank())
```
:::

On the z-scores:

- the one-standard-error and first-maximum rules of the gap statistic give **k = 1**, and **10**,
  the largest value tried, under the global maximum. The gap at k = 1 (`r round(tab[1, "gap"], 3)`)
  is not exceeded until k = 10 (`r round(tab[10, "gap"], 3)`), by much less than one standard error
  (about 0.04);
- the silhouette width is highest at **k = 2**, `r round(sil[1], 2)`, and stays between 0.22 and
  0.27 for every k. Kaufman and Rousseeuw's rule of thumb reads a width below 0.25 as no substantial
  structure;
- NbClust's majority vote is **2** (`r max(table(nb_z$Best.nc["Number_clusters", ]))` indices), with
  six chosen by `r sum(nb_z$Best.nc["Number_clusters", ] == 6)`.

The authors of the three references that fix a number of clusters use simpler methods. Rovan and
Sambt (2003, section 3.1) read the Ward dendrogram for "big jumps of the values of the between-group
sum of squares", and find two large jumps, at two and at four groups. Demeter and Brătucu (2013)
read cluster membership at two, three and four clusters from one tree and choose three for
interpretation. Brown and Watson (2012) apply the rule of thumb k = √(n/2), which for 55 townships
gives `r round(sqrt(55 / 2), 1)`. The first two readings are applied below to the Ward tree on
z-scores.

```{r}
#| fig-height: 3.2
merge_heights <- tibble(k = 2:10, height = rev(tree_z$height)[1:9]) |>
  mutate(jump = height - lead(height))

ggplot(merge_heights, aes(k, height)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point() +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(jump, 2)), vjust = -0.8, size = 3, na.rm = TRUE) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 2:10) +
  labs(y = "height of the merge that joins k clusters into k - 1")

nested <- sapply(2:6, \(k) cutree(tree_z, k))
colnames(nested) <- paste0("k", 2:6)
as_tibble(nested) |> count(k2, k3, k4, k5, k6)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
- `tree_z$height` holds the height of each merge in the order the merges were made, so its last
  value is the merge that joins the final two clusters. `rev()` reverses it, so element k − 1 is the
  height of the merge that joins k clusters into k − 1. `lead()` takes the next value, so `jump` is
  how much higher that merge is than the one before it, which joins k + 1 clusters into k. A large
  jump means that stopping at k clusters avoids an expensive merge.
- `cutree()` for k = 2 to 6 gives five columns of labels from the same tree, and `count()` lists
  each combination that occurs. Each row follows one group of townships down the tree, which is the
  reading of cluster membership that Demeter and Brătucu (2013) make at two, three and four
  clusters.
:::

The merge heights have secondary jumps at four and at six clusters. The largest jump is at two
clusters (`r round(merge_heights$jump[1], 2)`), and the next largest are at four
(`r round(merge_heights$jump[3], 2)`) and at six (`r round(merge_heights$jump[5], 2)`). From seven
clusters on, no jump exceeds `r round(max(merge_heights$jump[6:8]), 2)`. The nested table shows how
six arises: each of the two top-level groups divides into three, and no later split undoes an
earlier one.

The gap statistic gives one cluster; the silhouette width, NbClust and the largest merge-height jump
give two; the rule of thumb gives five; and the secondary merge-height jumps give four or six. The
ICT profiles of Shan's townships vary continuously, with weak separation between groups at any k, so
the number of regions cannot be settled by the data alone. De Souza and Taconeli (2022, section 3.3)
fix one k from the unconstrained Ward tree and use it "for all clustering algorithms henceforward",
so that the methods can be compared on equal terms. k = 6 is used in the same way in the rest of
Part 2: it is one of the break points of the tree, and it keeps the comparison with the chapter.

## Singleton regions in SKATER

Two of the six SKATER regions of section 3.2.4 are single townships. SKATER cuts the edge whose
removal most reduces the within-region sum of squares. A township whose values are far from all of
its neighbours' is expensive to keep attached, so cutting it off as a region of one is often the
best single cut. Assunção et al. (2006, section 4) met the same outcome in their own case study.
Their unrestricted regionalisation of the 96 districts of São Paulo into eight regions left "the
north-eastern region" with "one district only", 0.12% of the city's population, beside a region of
36 districts, and they note that "for many applications, this unbalance is not convenient". Their
remedy was a restriction on the regions: a minimum population of 500,000 inhabitants, under which
region populations ranged from 651,513 to 2,543,743. `spdep::skater()` implements the restriction
through its `crit` and `vec.crit` arguments, which its reference page, linked under "All About R",
describes as "limits of group size or limits of population size".

The question here is which townships become singletons on the standardised variables, and what a
minimum size, first in townships and then in households, does to the regions.

```{r}
skater_z <- function(crit = NULL, vec.crit = NULL, seed = 1234) {
  set.seed(seed)
  w <- nb2listw(shan.nb, nbcosts(shan.nb, as.data.frame(shan_ict.z)), style = "B")
  tree <- mstree(w)
  if (is.null(crit)) {
    spdep::skater(tree[, 1:2], as.data.frame(shan_ict.z), ncuts = 5)$groups
  } else if (is.null(vec.crit)) {
    spdep::skater(tree[, 1:2], as.data.frame(shan_ict.z), ncuts = 5, crit = crit)$groups
  } else {
    spdep::skater(tree[, 1:2], as.data.frame(shan_ict.z), ncuts = 5,
                  crit = crit, vec.crit = vec.crit)$groups
  }
}

sk_z <- skater_z()
sort(table(sk_z), decreasing = TRUE)
shan_sf$TS.x[sk_z %in% names(which(table(sk_z) == 1))]
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
- `skater_z()` repeats the three steps of section 3.2 on the z-scores: edge costs, minimum spanning
  tree, and SKATER. It returns the region of each township. `crit`, if given, is passed to
  `spdep::skater()` as a minimum per region. Without `vec.crit` the minimum counts townships; with
  `vec.crit`, a value for each township, the minimum applies to the sum of those values over the
  region.
- `names(which(table(sk_z) == 1))` finds the regions with one township, and the last line prints the
  names of those townships.
:::

On the standardised variables, three of the six regions are single townships: Muse, Tachileik and
Taunggyi. The singletons are the extremes on the variables with almost no weight before
standardising (section 4.2). Their z-scores on computer ownership are the three highest in the state
(`r paste(round(sort(shan_ict.z[, "COMPUTER_PR"], decreasing = TRUE)[1:3], 1), collapse = ", ")`).
Taunggyi is the state capital, and Muse and Tachileik are the main border crossings to China and
Thailand. The remaining 52 townships are divided into three large regions.

The singletons on both scales, in red:

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 5
singleton_map <- function(groups, title) {
  d <- mutate(shan_sf, region = factor(groups),
              single = groups %in% as.numeric(names(which(table(groups) == 1))))
  ggplot(d) +
    geom_sf(aes(fill = region), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2, alpha = 0.35) +
    geom_sf(data = d[d$single, ], fill = "red", colour = "black", linewidth = 0.4) +
    ggrepel::geom_label_repel(data = d[d$single, ], aes(label = TS.x, geometry = geometry),
                              stat = "sf_coordinates", size = 3, min.segment.length = 0,
                              nudge_x = 0.6) +
    scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2", guide = "none") +
    theme_void() + labs(title = title)
}
patchwork::wrap_plots(singleton_map(ccs6, "SKATER on the raw rates (section 3.2.4)"),
                      singleton_map(sk_z, "SKATER on z-scores"), ncol = 2)
```

Each of these singleton regions is a township that differs from every neighbour. A region of one
township, however, cannot be planned for as a region. The minimum size is set below to three and to
five townships:

```{r}
#| fig-height: 5
sk_z3 <- skater_z(crit = 3)
sk_z5 <- skater_z(crit = 5)

rbind(`no minimum` = unname(sort(table(sk_z), decreasing = TRUE)),
      `at least 3` = unname(sort(table(sk_z3), decreasing = TRUE)),
      `at least 5` = unname(sort(table(sk_z5), decreasing = TRUE)))

tmap_arrange(
  cluster_map(mutate(shan_sf, CLUSTER = factor(sk_z)), title = "SKATER, no minimum"),
  cluster_map(mutate(shan_sf, CLUSTER = factor(sk_z5)), title = "SKATER, at least 5"),
  ncol = 2)
```

```{r}
c(`no minimum` = ss_ratio(shan_ict.z, sk_z),
  `at least 3` = ss_ratio(shan_ict.z, sk_z3),
  `at least 5` = ss_ratio(shan_ict.z, sk_z5)) |> round(3)
```

With a minimum of five townships, the regions range from 5 to 14 townships, and the share of
variation explained falls from `r round(ss_ratio(shan_ict.z, sk_z), 2)`
to `r round(ss_ratio(shan_ict.z, sk_z5), 2)`. That loss is the cost of absorbing Muse, Tachileik and
Taunggyi into regions with neighbours that differ from them on computer ownership.

A minimum counted in townships gives a township of 3,318 households the same weight as Taunggyi with
82,604. Assunção et al. set their minimum in population, the quantity their regions were balanced
on. The equivalent here is a minimum number of households. Shan
has `r format(sum(shan_sf$TT_HOUSEHOLDS), big.mark = ",")` households, and minima of 50,000 and
100,000 are tried, roughly one twentieth and one tenth of the total.

```{r}
#| fig-height: 5
sk_hh50 <- skater_z(crit = 50000, vec.crit = shan_sf$TT_HOUSEHOLDS)
sk_hh100 <- skater_z(crit = 100000, vec.crit = shan_sf$TT_HOUSEHOLDS)

imap_dfr(list(`at least 50,000 households` = sk_hh50,
              `at least 100,000 households` = sk_hh100),
         \(g, name) tibble(minimum = name,
                           regions = length(unique(g)),
                           townships = paste(sort(table(g), decreasing = TRUE), collapse = ", "),
                           smallest_households = min(tapply(shan_sf$TT_HOUSEHOLDS, g, sum)),
                           explained = ss_ratio(shan_ict.z, g))) |>
  kable(digits = 3, format.args = list(big.mark = ","))

cluster_map(mutate(shan_sf, CLUSTER = factor(sk_hh100)),
            title = "SKATER, at least 100,000 households per region")
```

With a minimum of 50,000 households, Taunggyi remains a region of its own, because its 82,604
households meet the minimum by themselves. Muse and Tachileik are absorbed. With a minimum of
100,000, every region has between 7 and 12 townships, and the share explained
is `r round(ss_ratio(shan_ict.z, sk_hh100), 2)`, lower than with a minimum of five townships. As
Assunção et al. describe, the restriction balances the regions, here in households.

## Geographic dissimilarity in ClustGeo

The geographic matrix D1 of section 3.3.2 was built with `st_distance()` between polygons, and the
distance between two townships that share a boundary is zero. Chavent et al. (2018) illustrate two
kinds of D1: geographic distances between the municipalities (section 4.3), and a neighbourhood
matrix D1 = 1 − A, where A is the adjacency matrix with 1 on its diagonal (section 4.4). The
ClustGeo introduction page, linked under "All About R", specifies the first as "the distances
between the town halls of the 303 municipalities", that is, between points. The chapter's matrix
measures the distance between polygon boundaries, a third kind.

Two of the references use both kinds of D1 on one data set. Jaya et al. (2019) cluster diarrhoea
risk in the 30 districts of Bandung with a distance-based and a contiguity-based D1, and prefer the
distance-based one because diarrhoea may spread "not limited to adjacent locations but also possible
in locations that are far apart". De Souza and Taconeli (2022) run both versions on 399 Paraná
municipalities, choose α separately for each (0.25 for distances and 0.15 for neighbourhoods), and
find that the neighbourhood version separates the clusters more on the educational indicators. In
Jaya et al. and in de Souza and Taconeli, the choice of D1 is a decision about what "near" should
mean for the phenomenon, made before α is chosen.

The question here is what the chapter's D1 measures, and whether the two matrices from the paper
give more contiguous clusters at a smaller loss of homogeneity.

```{r}
A <- nb2mat(shan.nb, style = "B")
D1_poly <- as.matrix(distmat)
off_diag <- row(A) != col(A)

tibble(pairs_at_zero = sum(D1_poly[off_diag] == 0) / 2,
       neighbour_pairs = sum(A) / 2,
       zero_iff_neighbour = all((D1_poly == 0 & off_diag) == (A == 1)))
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
- `nb2mat(style = "B")` converts the neighbour list to a 55 × 55 matrix with 1 for neighbours and 0
  otherwise.
- `off_diag` is true everywhere except the diagonal. Pairs are counted in both directions in a full
  matrix, so each count is divided by 2.
- The last value tests whether a pair has zero distance exactly when the two townships are
  neighbours.
:::

The pairs with D1 = 0 are exactly the 132 neighbouring pairs. Under this D1, a township is at the
same distance, zero, from all of its neighbours, however large they are. Between townships that do
not touch, the distance is the gap between their nearest edges, so a long, thin township counts as
close to many others. The two alternatives from the paper are built below. Centroid distances need a
projected CRS, and Shan State is within UTM zone 47N (96°E to 102°E), EPSG:32647.

```{r}
shan_utm <- st_transform(shan_sf, 32647)
D1_centroid <- as.dist(st_distance(st_centroid(st_geometry(shan_utm))))

A1 <- A
diag(A1) <- 1
D1_neighbour <- as.dist(1 - A1)

D0_z <- dist(shan_ict.z)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
- `st_transform(shan_sf, 32647)` projects the layer to UTM zone 47N, in metres. `st_centroid()` then
  finds the centre of each township on the flat plane, and `st_distance()` between the centroids
  gives straight-line distances in metres.
- `D1_neighbour` follows section 4.4 of Chavent et al. (2018): the adjacency matrix with 1 on the
  diagonal, subtracted from 1. Neighbours are at dissimilarity 0 and all other pairs at 1.
- `D0_z` is the distance matrix on z-scores, used for all three versions of D1 so that only D1
  changes.
:::

::: callout-note
## What each D1 measures, for one township

The three maps show the dissimilarity between Taunggyi and every other township under each version
of D1:

- **Polygon distance (chapter):** every neighbour is at 0, however far its centre lies.
- **Centroid distance:** dissimilarity grows smoothly with distance.
- **Neighbourhood matrix, 1 − A:** neighbours are at 0, and every other township is at 1.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 3.6
ti <- which(shan_sf$TS.x == "Taunggyi")
d1_maps <- list(
  `polygon distance (km)` = as.matrix(distmat)[ti, ] / 1000,
  `centroid distance (km)` = as.matrix(D1_centroid)[ti, ] / 1000,
  `neighbourhood, 1 - A` = as.matrix(D1_neighbour)[ti, ])
d1_plots <- imap(d1_maps, \(v, name) {
  ggplot() + geom_sf(data = mutate(shan_sf, d = as.numeric(v)), aes(fill = d),
                     colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
    geom_sf(data = shan_sf[ti, ], fill = NA, colour = "red", linewidth = 0.6) +
    scale_fill_viridis_c(direction = -1) + theme_void() +
    labs(title = name, fill = NULL) + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
})
patchwork::wrap_plots(d1_plots, ncol = 3)
```

Taunggyi is outlined in red. On the first map, its neighbours have the same colour as Taunggyi
itself: the polygon distance gives every neighbour the same value, zero.
:::

For each D1, `choicealpha()` gives the two proportions for α from 0 to 1, and each partition's
pieces and share of variation explained are computed below.

```{r}
#| fig-height: 4
D1_list <- list(`polygon distance (chapter)` = distmat,
                `centroid distance` = D1_centroid,
                `neighbourhood 1 - A` = D1_neighbour)
alphas <- seq(0, 1, 0.1)

alpha_grid <- imap_dfr(D1_list, \(D1_mat, name) {
  cr <- choicealpha(D0_z, D1_mat, range.alpha = alphas, K = 6, graph = FALSE)
  parts <- lapply(alphas, \(a) cutree(hclustgeo(D0_z, D1_mat, alpha = a), 6))
  tibble(D1 = name, alpha = alphas,
         Q0norm = cr$Qnorm[, 1], Q1norm = cr$Qnorm[, 2],
         pieces = sapply(parts, count_pieces),
         explained = sapply(parts, \(g) ss_ratio(shan_ict.z, g)))
})

alpha_grid |>
  pivot_longer(c(Q0norm, Q1norm), names_to = "criterion", values_to = "value") |>
  ggplot(aes(alpha, value, linetype = criterion)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point(size = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ D1) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c(Q0norm = "solid", Q1norm = "dashed"),
                        labels = c("ICT variables (D0)", "geography (D1)")) +
  labs(y = "normalised proportion explained", linetype = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
- `imap_dfr()` calls the function once for each element of `D1_list`, passing the element as
  `D1_mat` and its name as `name`, and stacks the returned tables into one.
- For each D1 it runs `choicealpha()` without a chart, then for each α builds the six-cluster
  partition with `hclustgeo()` and computes its pieces and share of variation explained.
- The matrix is called `D1_mat` and not `D1` because `tibble()` builds its columns in order, and a
  later column can refer to an earlier one by name. A column named `D1` would then hide the matrix
  from the `pieces` and `explained` columns, and `hclustgeo()` would receive the text of the name.
- The chart is the lower panel of `choicealpha()`'s own output, read as in section 3.3.2, and drawn
  for the three versions of D1 together.
:::

```{r}
alpha_grid |>
  filter(alpha <= 0.6) |>
  select(D1, alpha, pieces, explained) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = D1, values_from = c(pieces, explained), names_vary = "slowest") |>
  kable(digits = 2)
```

- **Polygon distance.** The partition does not become contiguous in the range where α is useful. At
  α = 0.2 the six clusters are still
  in `r alpha_grid |> filter(D1 == "polygon distance (chapter)", alpha == 0.2) |> pull(pieces)`
  pieces. The chapter's own solution in section 3.3.3, on the raw rates, is
  in `r count_pieces(shan_sf_Gcluster$CLUSTER)`.
- **Centroid distance.** The partition has about as many pieces as with the polygon distance up to α
  = 0.3, and fewer above α = 0.3.
- **Neighbourhood matrix.** At α = 0.3 the partition has six pieces, which means six contiguous
  regions, and it
  explains `r alpha_grid |> filter(D1 == "neighbourhood 1 - A", alpha == 0.3) |> pull(explained) |> round(2)`
  of the variation.

With the neighbourhood matrix, contiguity is reached at the smallest α, which is the behaviour
Chavent et al. (2018) report for their data in section 4.4. Jaya et al. chose the distance-based D1
because diarrhoea spreads between districts that are far apart. By the same reasoning, the
neighbourhood matrix is the better choice for ICT access: ownership of a television or a telephone
does not spread between townships as an infection does, and a region is wanted here as an area that
can be administered as one.

Jaya et al. compare their two versions by their Q values at the chosen α. Q1 is computed on a
different matrix in each case, so a higher Q1 under one D1 does not mean more geographic cohesion
than a lower Q1 under another. The table above has no such mismatch: every version of D1 is scored
on the same two measures, the share of variation explained on the z-scores and the number of pieces.

Assunção et al. (2006, section 2) place ClustGeo's approach in a longer debate. They describe
methods that combine nearness in attribute space with nearness in geographic space as a weighted
mean, and report the criticism of Openshaw et al. (1998) that homogeneity and compactness "are not
strictly comparable" and that compactness "should not be combined with homogeneity measures", and
should be handled as a constraint. The mixing parameter α is such a weight, and in the table above
contiguity is not reached until α is large enough. In SKATER, REDCAP and AZP, contiguity is a
constraint.

## Methods from the lecture beyond the chapter

Slide 2 lists five spatially constrained methods, in two families. The hierarchical methods build
the regions by merging or by splitting a tree: SKATER, REDCAP and ClustGeo. The partitioning methods
start from a set of regions and improve it by moving townships between them: AZP and max-p. The
chapter covers SKATER and ClustGeo, run in sections 3.2 and 3.3. The `rgeoda` package, an R
interface to the GeoDa library, provides the others. The question here is how much of the variation
the remaining methods explain on Shan, and how balanced their regions are, against SKATER.

| Method | Family | How the regions are formed | Source |
|-------|------|--------------------------|-----------|
| **REDCAP** | hierarchical | builds a spanning tree by one of four linkages and cuts it as SKATER does; the full-order variants measure the dissimilarity between two clusters on all pairs of their townships, which addresses the SKATER limitation on slide 9; first-order single linkage is identical to SKATER | slides 9 to 12; Guo (2008) |
| **SCHC** (spatially constrained hierarchical clustering) | hierarchical | ordinary agglomerative clustering in which only neighbouring clusters may merge | not on the slides; provided by `rgeoda` beside REDCAP |
| **AZP** (automatic zoning procedure) | partitioning | starts from a random partition into k contiguous regions, and moves townships between neighbouring regions when a move reduces the within-region sum of squares and keeps every region contiguous; the greedy version stops at the first local optimum, and simulated annealing and tabu search accept some worse moves to escape one | slide 2; compared with SKATER in Assunção et al. (2006, section 5) |
| **max-p** | partitioning | takes a minimum per region, such as a number of households, in place of k, and finds the largest number of contiguous regions that all meet it | slide 2; Duque, Anselin and Rey (2012), not in the readings |

::: callout-note
## First-order and full-order linkage in REDCAP

Slide 9 describes two clusters, C1 with five members and C2 with three. There are 15 pairs of
members between them, and only three of the pairs are neighbours. First-order linkage measures the
distance between the clusters on the three neighbouring pairs only. Full-order linkage uses all 15.
SKATER is first-order, and slide 11 lists the six REDCAP variants, which differ in which pairs they
use and how they summarise them.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 3.4
angle <- c(A = 160, B = 115, C = 200, D = 240, E = 280, F = 310, G = 0, H = 55) * pi / 180
nodes <- tibble(id = names(angle), x = cos(angle), y = sin(angle),
                cluster = c(rep("C1", 5), rep("C2", 3)))
all_pairs <- expand_grid(a = nodes$id[1:5], b = nodes$id[6:8]) |>
  left_join(nodes, by = c(a = "id")) |> left_join(nodes, by = c(b = "id"), suffix = c("", "end"))
first_order <- all_pairs |> filter(paste0(a, b) %in% c("BH", "EH", "EF"))
linkage_panel <- function(pairs, title) {
  ggplot() +
    geom_segment(data = pairs, aes(x, y, xend = xend, yend = yend), colour = "red",
                 linewidth = 0.9) +
    geom_point(data = nodes, aes(x, y, fill = cluster), shape = 21, size = 8) +
    geom_text(data = nodes, aes(x, y, label = id)) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c(C1 = "lightblue", C2 = "moccasin")) +
    coord_equal(xlim = c(-1.25, 1.25), ylim = c(-1.25, 1.25)) + theme_void() +
    labs(title = title, fill = NULL) + theme(plot.margin = margin(5, 20, 5, 20))
}
patchwork::wrap_plots(linkage_panel(first_order, "First-order: 3 pairs (BH, EH, EF)"),
                      linkage_panel(all_pairs, "Full-order: all 15 pairs"),
                      ncol = 2, guides = "collect")
```

The eight members are placed on a circle so that no line passes through a third member. Their
positions are for illustration and are not those of the slide.
:::

### Contiguity in rgeoda

`rgeoda` builds its own weights from the polygons. Two townships count as Queen neighbours when
their boundaries share a point, and `queen_weights()` tests whether two vertices are the same point
by a precision threshold, zero by default. When adjacent polygons in a shapefile were digitised
separately, their shared boundary may have vertices that differ in the last decimal places, and an
exact comparison then misses the link. `rgeoda`'s neighbours are compared below with those of
`poly2nb()` in section 3.2.1, with and without a threshold.

```{r}
queen_default <- queen_weights(shan_sf)
queen_matched <- queen_weights(shan_sf, precision_threshold = 1e-7)

tibble(weights = c("spdep::poly2nb()", "rgeoda default", "rgeoda, precision_threshold = 1e-7"),
       links = c(sum(card(shan.nb)),
                 sum(sapply(1:55, \(i) length(get_neighbors(queen_default, i)))),
                 sum(sapply(1:55, \(i) length(get_neighbors(queen_matched, i))))),
       min_neighbours_reported = c(min(card(shan.nb)), min_neighbors(queen_default),
                                   min_neighbors(queen_matched))) |>
  kable()

all(sapply(1:55, \(i) setequal(get_neighbors(queen_matched, i), shan.nb[[i]])))
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
```r
queen_weights(sf_obj, order = 1, precision_threshold = 0)  # rgeoda
get_neighbors(gda_w, idx)                                  # rgeoda
min_neighbors(gda_w)                                       # rgeoda
```

- `queen_weights()` finds Queen neighbours. With `precision_threshold = 0` two boundary points must
  be exactly equal to count as shared. A positive threshold, here 1e-7 degrees (about 1 cm), counts
  points closer than that as shared.
- `get_neighbors()` returns the neighbours of township `idx`, and `length()` counts them.
- `min_neighbors()` returns the smallest number of neighbours of any township, as `rgeoda` records
  it in the weights object.
- The last line tests whether the matched weights give every township exactly the same neighbours as
  `spdep`.
:::

With exact matching, `rgeoda` misses nine links, including four of Pangsang's five neighbours,
because the boundaries of adjacent townships in this shapefile do not share exactly identical
vertices. The weights object records a minimum of zero neighbours, which `rgeoda` records as an
isolated township. In testing, `rgeoda::skater()` on the default weights crashed the R session. With
a threshold of 1e-7 degrees, the neighbours are the same as `spdep`'s for every township, and those
weights are used for all the methods below.

### Running the methods

`rgeoda` standardises the variables to z-scores by default (`scale_method = "standardize"`), so the
raw rates are passed and the results are comparable with the z-score results above.

```{r}
rs <- 123456789
rg <- list(
  `SKATER (rgeoda)` = rgeoda::skater(6, queen_matched, shan_ict, random_seed = rs, cpu_threads = 1),
  `REDCAP first-order single` = redcap(6, queen_matched, shan_ict, "firstorder-singlelinkage",
                                       random_seed = rs, cpu_threads = 1),
  `REDCAP full-order single` = redcap(6, queen_matched, shan_ict, "fullorder-singlelinkage",
                                      random_seed = rs, cpu_threads = 1),
  `REDCAP full-order average` = redcap(6, queen_matched, shan_ict, "fullorder-averagelinkage",
                                       random_seed = rs, cpu_threads = 1),
  `REDCAP full-order complete` = redcap(6, queen_matched, shan_ict, "fullorder-completelinkage",
                                        random_seed = rs, cpu_threads = 1),
  `REDCAP full-order Ward` = redcap(6, queen_matched, shan_ict, "fullorder-wardlinkage",
                                    random_seed = rs, cpu_threads = 1),
  `SCHC Ward` = schc(6, queen_matched, shan_ict, "ward"),
  `AZP greedy` = azp_greedy(6, queen_matched, shan_ict, random_seed = rs),
  `AZP simulated annealing` = azp_sa(6, queen_matched, shan_ict, cooling_rate = 0.85,
                                     random_seed = rs),
  `AZP tabu` = azp_tabu(6, queen_matched, shan_ict, tabu_length = 10, conv_tabu = 10,
                        random_seed = rs))

rg_table <- imap_dfr(rg, \(r, name) tibble(
  method = name,
  explained = r$`The ratio of between to total sum of squares`,
  pieces = count_pieces(r$Clusters),
  sizes = paste(sort(table(r$Clusters), decreasing = TRUE), collapse = ", ")))
kable(rg_table, digits = 3)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
```r
rgeoda::skater(k, w, df, random_seed, cpu_threads)        # rgeoda
redcap(k, w, df, method, random_seed, cpu_threads)        # rgeoda
schc(k, w, df, method)                                    # rgeoda
azp_greedy(p, w, df, random_seed)                         # rgeoda
azp_sa(p, w, df, cooling_rate, random_seed)               # rgeoda
azp_tabu(p, w, df, tabu_length, conv_tabu, random_seed)   # rgeoda
```

- Every function takes the number of regions, the weights and the data, and returns a list with
  `$Clusters`, the region of each township, and the ratio of between to total sum of squares.
- `method` in `redcap()` names the linkage and the order of constraint. In `schc()` it names the
  linkage.
- `cooling_rate` sets how quickly simulated annealing stops accepting worse moves. `tabu_length`
  sets how many recent moves tabu search forbids reversing, and `conv_tabu` how many moves without
  improvement end the search.
- `random_seed` fixes the random start of the tree or the partition, and `cpu_threads = 1` makes the
  result independent of the number of processor cores.
- `rgeoda::` is written in full for `skater()`, because `spdep` has a function of the same name.
:::

The regions of every method are in six pieces, so all of them are strictly contiguous. They differ
in how much of the variation their regions explain and in how balanced the regions are:

| Methods | Share explained | Singletons | Note |
|------|--|--|----------|
| SKATER (`rgeoda`); REDCAP first-order single | `r sprintf("%.2f", rg_table$explained[1])` | 3 | identical regions, as on slide 10; different regions from `spdep`'s SKATER on the same z-scores (adjusted Rand index `r round(adjustedRandIndex(rg[[1]]$Clusters, sk_z), 2)`), which also has three singletons |
| REDCAP full-order single | `r sprintf("%.2f", rg_table$explained[3])` | 2 | the lowest of the REDCAP variants |
| REDCAP full-order average, complete, Ward | 0.51 to 0.52 | 1 or 2 | the highest of the tree-based methods |
| SCHC Ward | `r sprintf("%.2f", rg_table$explained[7])` | 5 | one region of 50 townships |
| AZP greedy, simulated annealing, tabu | 0.50 to 0.51 | 1 | from a random start; greedy and tabu search give the same share and region sizes |

Assunção et al. (2006, section 5) compare SKATER with AZP on three Brazilian data sets and find
SKATER "superior to AZP in all tests", with AZP's partition quality between 0.678 and 0.988 of
SKATER's. On Shan the order is reversed: AZP explains more than either SKATER implementation. The
authors themselves caution that "there is no decisive way to compare two classification methods,
because performance is dependent on the characteristics of the data set", and their AZP was run five
times from different starts with the best kept, where the runs here use one seed. The single
comparison here is consistent with that caution. On 55 units with weak spatial structure (section
4.1), SKATER's first cuts separate the extreme townships, and AZP's moves of townships between
neighbouring regions give a higher share explained.

### Max-p with a household threshold
