Max-p fixes a minimum number of households per region and finds the largest number of contiguous
regions that meet it. It is listed on slide 2 and is not used in the readings; the method is from
Duque, Anselin and Rey (2012). Shan has `r format(sum(shan_sf$TT_HOUSEHOLDS), big.mark = ",")`
households. The threshold is set to 100,000 and 150,000 households, roughly one tenth and one
seventh of the total.

```{r}
#| fig-height: 5
hh <- shan_sf["TT_HOUSEHOLDS"]
maxp_100 <- maxp_greedy(queen_matched, shan_ict, bound_variable = hh, min_bound = 100000,
                        iterations = 99, random_seed = rs, cpu_threads = 1)
maxp_150 <- maxp_greedy(queen_matched, shan_ict, bound_variable = hh, min_bound = 150000,
                        iterations = 99, random_seed = rs, cpu_threads = 1)

imap_dfr(list(`at least 100,000` = maxp_100, `at least 150,000` = maxp_150),
         \(r, name) tibble(threshold = name,
                           regions = length(unique(r$Clusters)),
                           explained = r$`The ratio of between to total sum of squares`,
                           sizes = paste(sort(table(r$Clusters), decreasing = TRUE),
                                         collapse = ", "))) |>
  kable(digits = 3)

tmap_arrange(
  cluster_map(mutate(shan_sf, CLUSTER = factor(maxp_100$Clusters)),
              title = "max-p, at least 100,000 households"),
  cluster_map(mutate(shan_sf, CLUSTER = factor(maxp_150$Clusters)),
              title = "max-p, at least 150,000 households"),
  ncol = 2)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
```r
maxp_greedy(w, df, bound_variable, min_bound, iterations, random_seed, cpu_threads)  # rgeoda
```

- `bound_variable` is a one-column sf data frame holding the quantity that each region must reach,
  here the number of households, and `min_bound` is the threshold.
- `iterations = 99` runs the construction phase 99 times from different random starts and keeps the
  best result.
- Max-p determines the number of regions from the threshold.
:::

A threshold of 150,000 households gives six regions, the same number as the other methods, with no
singletons: every region has at least `r min(table(maxp_150$Clusters))` townships. The share
explained is lower, `r round(maxp_150[["The ratio of between to total sum of squares"]], 2)`,
because under the threshold, townships as different as Taunggyi and its rural neighbours have to
share a region.

## Comparison of the regionalisations

Part 1 has three sets of six clusters, from Ward, SKATER and ClustGeo, and sections 4.2 to 4.7 have
seven more. Slides 4 and 5 show scattered and contiguous clusters side by side. Conventional
clustering finds the most homogeneous groups without regard to contiguity. The constrained methods
guarantee or encourage contiguity, and their groups are less homogeneous. Every set of six clusters
on this page is scored below on the two measures, computed on the same standardised variables.

```{r}
comparison <- bind_rows(
  tibble(method = "Hierarchical, raw rates, ward.D (chapter, 3.1.12)",
         groups = list(as.integer(shan_sf_cluster$CLUSTER))),
  tibble(method = "Hierarchical, z-scores, ward.D2 (4.2)", groups = list(h_z)),
  tibble(method = "SKATER, raw rates (chapter, 3.2)", groups = list(ccs6)),
  tibble(method = "SKATER, z-scores (4.5)", groups = list(sk_z)),
  tibble(method = "SKATER, z-scores, at least 5 (4.5)", groups = list(sk_z5)),
  tibble(method = "ClustGeo, raw, polygon D1, alpha 0.2 (chapter, 3.3)",
         groups = list(as.integer(shan_sf_Gcluster$CLUSTER))),
  tibble(method = "ClustGeo, z, neighbourhood D1, alpha 0.3 (4.6)",
         groups = list(cutree(hclustgeo(D0_z, D1_neighbour, alpha = 0.3), 6))),
  tibble(method = "REDCAP full-order complete (4.7)",
         groups = list(rg$`REDCAP full-order complete`$Clusters)),
  tibble(method = "AZP tabu (4.7)", groups = list(rg$`AZP tabu`$Clusters)),
  tibble(method = "max-p, 150,000 households (4.7)", groups = list(maxp_150$Clusters))) |>
  mutate(explained = map_dbl(groups, \(g) ss_ratio(shan_ict.z, g)),
         pieces = map_dbl(groups, count_pieces),
         smallest = map_dbl(groups, \(g) min(table(g))))

comparison |> select(-groups) |> kable(digits = 2)
```

```{r}
#| fig-height: 5
ggplot(comparison, aes(pieces, explained, label = str_remove(method, " \\(.*"))) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5, colour = "steelblue") +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(size = 3, max.overlaps = 20) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 6, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  annotate("text", x = 6.3, y = 0.3, label = "six contiguous regions", hjust = 0, size = 3,
           colour = "grey40") +
  labs(x = "number of separate pieces in the six clusters",
       y = "share of variation explained (z-scores)")
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
- Each row of `comparison` holds a method name and, in a list column, its vector of cluster labels.
  `map_dbl()` applies each measure to every vector. `smallest` is the size of the smallest region.
- `geom_text_repel()` from `ggrepel` places the labels so they do not overlap each other or the
  points. The dashed line marks six pieces, the value for six contiguous regions.
:::

Each point is one set of six clusters. Points further right are in more pieces, and points higher up
explain more of the variation. The dashed line marks six pieces, which means six contiguous regions.

- **Contiguity costs about a quarter of the explained variation.** Unconstrained Ward clustering on
  z-scores explains `r round(comparison$explained[2], 2)` and its clusters are
  in `r comparison$pieces[2]` pieces. The best strictly contiguous solutions, REDCAP full-order and
  AZP, explain about 0.51.
- **The chapter's two constrained solutions are not the strongest.** SKATER on raw rates
  explains `r round(comparison$explained[3], 2)` on the standardised measure, with two singletons,
  and the chapter's ClustGeo solution explains `r round(comparison$explained[6], 2)` while its
  clusters are still in `r comparison$pieces[6]` pieces.
- **Balanced regions cost more.** The solutions with no singletons, SKATER with a minimum of five,
  ClustGeo with the neighbourhood matrix, and max-p, explain between 0.36 and 0.41.

REDCAP full-order complete linkage gives the most homogeneous contiguous regions. Its regions,
profiled by their mean rates:

```{r}
#| fig-height: 5
redcap_sf <- shan_sf |> mutate(REGION = factor(rg$`REDCAP full-order complete`$Clusters))
cluster_map(redcap_sf, "REGION", "REDCAP full-order complete linkage, six regions")
```

```{r}
redcap_sf |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  group_by(REGION) |>
  summarise(townships = n(),
            households = sum(TT_HOUSEHOLDS),
            across(RADIO_PR:COMPUTER_PR, mean),
            members = if (n() <= 3) paste(TS.x, collapse = ", ") else "") |>
  kable(digits = 0, format.args = list(big.mark = ","))
```

```{r}
#| fig-height: 4
redcap_sf |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  select(REGION, RADIO_PR:COMPUTER_PR) |>
  bind_cols(as_tibble(shan_ict.z) |> rename_with(\(x) paste0(x, "_z"))) |>
  select(REGION, ends_with("_z")) |>
  pivot_longer(-REGION, names_to = "variable", values_to = "z") |>
  mutate(variable = str_remove(variable, "_PR_z")) |>
  ggplot(aes(variable, z)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "light blue") +
  facet_grid(~ REGION) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "z-score") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```

The profile is drawn on z-scores, so that the five variables share one scale and a box above the
zero line means a region above the state average.

Brown and Watson (2012) express each cluster mean as a percentage of the mean across all units, and
describe the clusters by variables that "were not used in the cluster analysis". De Souza and
Taconeli (2022, section 4) cross-tabulate their clusters against the official intermediate regions
of Paraná, and compare the clusters on each indicator by an F test. Rovan and Sambt (2003) name
their clusters from the mean profiles. Two variables were left out of the clustering for Shan,
internet at home (dropped in section 3.1.4) and the number of households, and the state has an
official division into three parts.

```{r}
state_mean <- redcap_sf |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  summarise(across(c(RADIO_PR:INTERNET_PR, TT_HOUSEHOLDS), mean))

redcap_sf |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  group_by(REGION) |>
  summarise(townships = n(), across(c(RADIO_PR:INTERNET_PR, TT_HOUSEHOLDS), mean)) |>
  mutate(across(c(RADIO_PR:INTERNET_PR, TT_HOUSEHOLDS), \(x) 100 * x / state_mean[[cur_column()]])) |>
  rename_with(\(x) str_remove(x, "_PR"), RADIO_PR:INTERNET_PR) |>
  kable(digits = 0, caption = "Region means as a percentage of the state mean. INTERNET and TT_HOUSEHOLDS were not used to form the regions")
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
- `state_mean` holds the mean of each rate over all 55 townships.
- In the second block of code, `summarise()` computes the region means, and `mutate(across(...))`
  divides each by the state mean of the same column. `cur_column()` returns the name of the column
  being processed, so each column is divided by its own state mean. A value of 100 is the state
  average.
:::

```{r}
table(part = redcap_sf$ST, region = redcap_sf$REGION)
chisq.test(table(redcap_sf$ST, redcap_sf$REGION), simulate.p.value = TRUE, B = 9999)$p.value

map_dfr(c("RADIO_PR", "TV_PR", "LLPHONE_PR", "MPHONE_PR", "COMPUTER_PR"), \(v) {
  f <- summary(aov(redcap_sf[[v]] ~ redcap_sf$REGION))[[1]]
  tibble(rate = v, F = f$`F value`[1], p_value = format.pval(f$`Pr(>F)`[1], digits = 2))
}) |>
  kable(digits = 1)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
- `table()` counts the townships of each part of the state in each region.
  `chisq.test(simulate.p.value = TRUE)` tests whether regions and parts are independent. Several
  cells are small, so the p-value is taken from 9,999 simulated tables and not from the chi-squared
  approximation.
- `aov()` fits a one-way analysis of variance of each rate on the region, and `summary()` returns
  the F statistic and its p-value. The five rates are tested one at a time, as in de Souza and
  Taconeli (2022).
:::

The six regions differ significantly on every one of the five rates, most strongly on land line.
These F tests are descriptive only: the regions were formed to differ on the same five variables, so
significant differences are expected by construction. Internet at home and the official division of
the state were not used to form the regions.

::: callout-note
## What the F test compares

For one rate, the F test compares how far apart the six region means are with how spread out the
townships are inside the regions:

$$F = \frac{\text{difference between the region means}}{\text{spread of the townships inside the regions}}$$

- **A large F:** the region means are far apart, and the townships in each region are close to their
  region mean. The regions differ on that rate.
- **A small F:** the differences between the region means are small compared with the spread inside
  the regions.
- **The p-value** is the probability of an F at least this large if all six regions had the same
  mean.

Each part of the formula is a sum of squares divided by its degrees of freedom: 6 − 1 = 5 for the
region means and 55 − 6 = 49 for the townships inside the regions.
:::

Internet at home, which was dropped in section 3.1.4 for its correlation with computer ownership, is
close to computer ownership in five of the six regions: both are 165% of the state mean in region 2,
and the Taunggyi region is highest on both. The exception is region 4, where computer ownership is
close to average (92%) and internet at home is half of it (49%). Apart from Laukkaing, Konkyan and
Kunlong (region 4), little information was lost by dropping internet. The regions are also
associated with the official parts of the state (simulated p < 0.01): region 2 is in Shan (East) and
Shan (North), region 3 in Shan (North) and Shan (South), and the three small regions in Shan (North)
or Shan (South). Only the largest region spans all three parts.

Named from their profiles, in the manner of Rovan and Sambt (2003), the six regions are:

| Region | Townships | Name | Profile, as a percentage of the state mean |
|--|--|-----|------------|
| 1 | 24 | Low access | below the state mean on every item, from 55% (land line) to 88% (radio) |
| 2 | 14 | Connected east and north | 154% to 165% on land line, mobile phone, computer and internet |
| 3 | 11 | High radio | radio 158%, TV and mobile phone close to average, land line and computer about 70%; the second-largest townships on average (136% of mean households) |
| 4 | 3 | Land line, low radio | Laukkaing, Konkyan and Kunlong: land line 317%, radio 30% |
| 5 | 2 | Low TV and computer | Narphan and Pangwaun: TV 57%, computer 19%, internet 11% |
| 6 | 1 | Taunggyi | the state capital, above average on everything and 450% of mean households |

# Reflection

Chapter 12 asks, in section 12.2.1, whether Shan State can be delineated into homogeneous regions
using six ICT measures. The answer on this page is yes, with qualifications that the chapter does
not raise.

**The regions depend on the scale of the variables.** On the raw rates, mobile phone and TV make up
81% of the distance, so the chapter's clusters group the townships mainly on those two. After
standardising, the SKATER singletons change from Ywangan and Narphan to Taunggyi, Muse and
Tachileik.

**The number of regions is not settled by the data.** The gap statistic, the silhouette width and
NbClust all give fewer than six clusters, and the silhouette widths show weak structure at every k.
The merge heights of the Ward tree jump at two, four and six clusters. I would report the six
regions as one level of a nested partition, with the two- and four-region levels beside it.

**Most of the rates have no spatial pattern.** De Souza and Taconeli (2022) found every one of their
indicators spatially autocorrelated; here only radio and land line are. TV and mobile phone, which
carry most of the weight in the chapter's clusters, have no significant pattern. That explains the
fragmented map of section 3.1.12 better than the omission of location from the method, and it is why
contiguity costs about a quarter of the explained variation in section 4.8.

**SKATER is not the strongest method on these data.** Before section 4.8, I expected SKATER to be
the natural choice, because it is contiguous by construction and taught first. REDCAP full-order and
AZP explain more, consistent with the SKATER limitation on slide 9, and without a minimum size three
of SKATER's six regions are single townships. Assunção et al. (2006) met the same problem in São
Paulo and set a minimum population; here a minimum of 100,000 households gives six regions of 7 to
12 townships. They also found SKATER better than AZP on every data set they tried. On Shan the order
is reversed, which fits their own remark that performance "is dependent on the characteristics of
the data set".

Three calls in the chapter ran without error and without the effect that the text around them
describes:

- the standardised versions of the data were computed and not used for clustering;
- `hclust(method = "ward.D")` was run where the agglomerative coefficient that justified it belongs
  to `ward.D2`;
- `st_distance()` between polygons gave a geographic matrix in which all neighbours are at distance
  zero.

As in chapters 9 and 10, one object is computed and a different object is passed to the next step.
All three faults are explained in the course's own sources. The UC Business Analytics tutorial, the
source of chapter sections 12.7.8 to 12.7.10, standardises with `scale()` and uses `ward.D2`, and
Chavent et al. (2018) describe what `hclustgeo()` computes and offer the neighbourhood matrix as D1.

**Limits.** Population is not weighted in most of the methods: apart from max-p and the household
minimum in section 4.5, a township of 3,318 households counts as much as Taunggyi with 82,604. The
weights argument of `hclustgeo()` (Chavent et al., 2018, section 2.2) could give households a weight
in ClustGeo. The data are from the 2014 census, so the regions are based on access as it was in
2014.

# About this document

Written and executed in Quarto with R `r getRversion()`, `spdep` `r packageVersion("spdep")`,
`ClustGeo` `r packageVersion("ClustGeo")`, `rgeoda` `r packageVersion("rgeoda")` and
`tmap` `r packageVersion("tmap")`. All figures and tables are generated at render time from the data
in `data/`, so nothing on this page is pasted in.

I used AI assistance while working out the approach and the extensions in Part 2. The analysis was
run and checked by me.
